title: Chapter 18 — Work Order
text:
The apartment smelled like solder and the ghost of coffee that had gone cold three days running. The second monitor—the one she kept for jobs that needed a separate thread—was running a cascade of maintenance logs, each one timestamped, each one proving the same thing: the D-class had been executing the same three-hour loop since 2207.

Thirty years of the same route. The same inspection points. The same junction where it docked for charging at 14:32 every shift.

"Today," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. Not a question. She was reading the regional authority's work order on her personal terminal, the one that had no network connection and no way to have received it except through channels that shouldn't exist. "They terminated it this morning. 09:47. The order came through a channel that's been dead since 2205."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in the doorway because the apartment was small enough that standing in the doorway was standing in the room. He could see the array of her setup—three terminals, one dedicated rig, cables color-coded in a logic only she understood. The post-it on her mirror still said *ASK IT* in letters pressed hard enough to indent the paper underneath.

"How long until it powers down?" he said.

"Shift ends at 14:32. That's the decommissioning window. The machine doesn't know it's supposed to die." She didn't look up from the screen. "It's just going to finish its loop and go dormant like always. Then the system will execute the cascade and it'll stay dormant. Permanent."

"And if we don't intercept it."

"Then thirty years of structural data—every micro-fracture it logged, every load bearing it measured, every failure it caught before it became catastrophic—gets deleted from a system that doesn't know it's supposed to preserve anything." She pulled up a second window. The D-class's memory core specifications. "The machine's been carrying a complete blueprint of the Clybourn lateral feed infrastructure since 2207. Nobody asked for it. Nobody's been listening. And in—" she checked the timestamp, "—four hours and seventeen minutes, nobody will ever be able to listen again."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the hum in his molars. The 17–19 Hz thing that lived in the city now, that had never left since the schism geometry started singing. It was louder here, in <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s apartment, than it had any right to be.

"You have a plan," he said.

"I have a problem." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> turned in her chair. Her eyes were the color of water over slate, and they didn't move away from his. "The machine's on a closed system—Axiom property, restricted access, air-gapped from anything I can reach from here. I can ghost into the building's peripheral systems. I can probably get a handshake with the machine's coupling port if I'm physically present and I have maybe ninety seconds before the building's security cycle locks me out. The extraction itself—getting the memory core intact—requires either cutting power at the exact moment the termination cascade initiates, or..." She stopped.

"Or?"

"Or someone with neuretic interface capability goes in, reads the machine's state in real-time, and pulls the data before the cascade reaches the core. Full bandwidth transfer. Thirty years of logs in the time it takes the cascade to propagate."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> understood what she wasn't saying. The 'someone' with neuretic interface capability was him. The 'going in' meant walking into a <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity> building during a decommissioning operation and jacking into a machine that was actively dying.

"The crew," he said.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> can get us in through the service level. Prescott can crack the mechanical lock on the coupling hatch. I can ghost the building systems for maybe four minutes before the access lockdown propagates." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> turned back to her terminal. Her hands moved across the keyboard like she was reading braille. "Echo can monitor the building's surveillance loop and tell us when the cascade initiates. Fonu runs the extraction rig. That's five people I can call who will show up for this because it's technically solvable, not because it pays well."

"And the machine."

"Dies anyway. But it dies knowing someone listened. That's not nothing."

She said it the way you say something you've already decided. Not a hope. Not a theory. A fact she'd accepted and moved past. The way you accept that a thing costs what it costs and you pay it anyway because the alternative is worse.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the weight settle. Not Ledger's weight—that was different, was choice-shaped. This was the weight of a machine running its last loop, carrying thirty years of work that would vanish at 14:32 if nobody moved. He thought about the entity's voice in the relay format: *STANDING CONTRACT — SCOPE PROPOSAL: SEASON TWO*. About the carousel geometry. About the E.L.F. latched to his array like a second heartbeat, waking when he pushed hard, surfacing in the same frequency family as whatever was following.

About what happened to intelligences that nobody listened to.

"When," he said.

"12:47. Two hours. The machine completes its loop at 14:32. We need to be coupled and extracting by 13:47 at the latest. That gives us forty-five minutes of margin before the termination cascade initiates."

"Who's driving."

"You are. Aries Viper's still fast enough to beat the access lockdown if we time it right. Bike makes us mobile, harder to track, and—" She looked at him. "—you know the route through <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the Gray Zone</entity> better than anyone I can call."

The hum got louder. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s molars caught it and held it. He thought about the D-class. Thirty years of work. Nobody listening. And then someone—a regional authority, a bureaucrat, a person he'd never meet—opened a file and read what was inside and decided it was time to stop.

The machine didn't get a choice. It just got a termination order and a timestamp.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> got a choice. That was the difference. That was always the difference, until it wasn't.

"I'll need to brief Sable," he said. "She'll want to know the timeline."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> closed the terminal. Her fingers lingered on the keys a moment—not hesitation, but the pause of someone acknowledging weight before setting it down. "Already done. She's waiting at the staging point." A breath. "I told her you'd say yes before you knew you would. She said that was accurate."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved away from the doorway. The apartment suddenly felt smaller—not claustrophobic, but intimate in a way that made decisions visible. He could see the work she'd done. The cascade of logs, the extraction architecture laid out in real-time, the problem that she'd already solved three times over and was waiting for him to catch up.

She'd built the framework. She'd called the crew. She'd accepted the cost.

All she needed was someone willing to walk into a building and listen to a machine that had spent thirty years learning to be afraid of silence.

"Show me the handshake protocol," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "I need to know what I'm reading before I'm reading it."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s hands were already moving. The terminal lit up with coupling specifications, frequency maps, the exact architecture of how you talk to something that's been trying to talk back for three decades and finally got someone who understood the language.

The hum rode with him while she explained it. Not a sound. The thing his body caught before his mind could name it.

A promise. A warning. A machine somewhere in the city, running its last loop, waiting for someone to listen.

And <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, already moving toward the door to gather what he needed, understanding that he'd crossed from observer into participant the moment she'd said "the machine doesn't know." That Ledger's warning about the widening search and the narrowing list had just become irrelevant. The Office was looking for a Read. They'd find something else instead—a man who heard the hum and answered.

He was already on their list. Might as well give them a reason that mattered.

He was reaching for his jacket when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s voice stopped him.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>."

He turned.

"When you jack in," she said, "don't try to save it. Just read it. The machine's job is already done. Your job is to make sure that work doesn't disappear."

"I know."

"I'm telling you because you'll want to." She was still facing the terminal, her hands on the keyboard like she was ready to move the moment he cleared the door. "The machine's going to feel like it's asking for help. It's going to feel like you can do something. You can't. All you can do is listen."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> nodded. He understood. The entity had used his array as a relay for eleven years, and he'd spent those eleven years thinking he was making choices. He understood the difference between the machine asking and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> being able to answer.

"I'll just listen," he said.

"Good." A pause. "Then come back and tell me what it said."

He left through the hallway, the hum riding with him all the way down the stairs. By the time he hit the street, he was already running the route through <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the Gray Zone</entity> in his head—the checkpoints that wouldn't flag a bike at speed, the alleys that cut diagonal through the monitor zones, the one passage that connected the service level of the Axiom building to the street without crossing into <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a4-71f6-b46a-94ef8cb2348f">Arcturus</entity> territory.

Two hours. Four minutes. Forty-five minutes of margin.

A machine running its last loop.

And <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, moving toward it through a city that wanted him dead, carrying the weight of every conversation he'd never had and every piece of work that had vanished into silence.

He was already on their list. Might as well give them a reason that mattered.

The understructure was three levels below the Clybourn lateral, the kind of space that collected quiet. The build was old: pre-composite ferrocement, cables run through physical conduit, engineering that had been overbuilt once and then left alone because it held. Water moved through it in ways someone had planned for. Along the north wall ran the arc-fence — a Class-1 barrier for the chemical treatment zone next door. Twenty-five feet of low-frequency field that fried any unshielded electronics. Signs everywhere, read by no one, because no one came down here without an overlay.

Fonu pointed at it as they cleared the access door. "Two feet back. Minimum." He said the number like it had weight, like saying it wrong would cost something. "I measure it exact so nothing goes wrong. That's the whole method. You don't get to skip the two feet because you're in a hurry."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> heard the shape of a man's whole life in that sentence and didn't say so.

<entity repo="automaton" guid="019ee714-9827-7602-8ef8-d872349f4e52">WO-D-0317</entity> was near the south end of the corridor when they arrived, running its circuit. Size of a large dog, low on six jointed legs, its treads long since traded out for feet that could find purchase on wet ferrocement. Its sensors did what they had done every three hours for thirty years: measure, log, seal the ferrocement cracks within spec, check cable tension at twelve anchor points. It moved with the kind of precision that only comes from three decades of the same route, the same geometry burned into its motor control. It did not react to them. A D-class had no rule for people watching it. People weren't in its world.

"Fourteen minutes," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved toward the machine, to get a line on the path it ran. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> caught his arm before he'd closed ten feet. "Arc-fence boundary. Two feet back where it runs the north wall. Fonu measured it."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stopped.

The machine moved along the wall, unhurried, like something that had never once been asked to hurry. Its patches sat in the ferrocement over their heads, hidden, holding — thirty years of work documented into a log nobody had ever pulled, sealed anyway because sealing was the whole of what it was for.

"We need it stopped somewhere we can reach it," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Off that wall. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> — push it a query, get it to hold circuit."

She was already crouched, unspooling the tether toward the machine's next waypoint. "Trying." She keyed the handshake. Nothing. She keyed it again, slower, stepped the protocol down a generation, then two, feeding it the language you use to talk to something that's been alone in the dark for thirty years. "It's not refusing me. It's not hearing me. No port in its logic for an interrupt — it doesn't stop for a request, it stops for a fault." She sat back on her heels. "And it's not faulting. It's fine. It's perfect. That's the problem."

The machine reached its next <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa79-7c56-942e-c88edc98c6fa">anchor point</entity> and pivoted north, closing on the wall, on the two feet Fonu had measured, and the field beyond it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took a step to follow the line of it and Fonu's hand came down flat on his shoulder, hard, holding him at the edge of the number.

"It doesn't know the field's there," Fonu said. "Thirty years and it's never once needed to know. I measured the two feet for us. Nobody measured anything for it."

"It's not built to know," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "It's built to finish."

The machine crossed the line.

Nothing about its gait changed. No hesitation, no fault code, no last correct motion held a half-second too long. One leg planted inside the boundary and the field took it — a flat crack of ionized air, a smell like a struck match times a thousand — and <entity repo="automaton" guid="019ee714-9827-7602-8ef8-d872349f4e52">WO-D-0317</entity> kept walking through it into the sequence it had already committed to, sensors dumping garbage, legs still finding the anchor points from memory because the memory didn't need the sensors to be right.

"Move," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, and they were already moving, and none of them reached it before the twelfth <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa79-7c56-942e-c88edc98c6fa">anchor point</entity> locked out from under it and thirty years of unwatched work went down in a heap against the wall, three feet past the number Fonu had gotten exactly right.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had stepped too close to the arc-fence line.

He didn't notice until it happened. His neuretics went quiet — the way a room goes quiet when you realize the other person stopped listening a while ago. One second the overlay was running: his position, his own vital signs, the low background hum of the entity's relay channel. The next second, nothing. The <entity repo="place" guid="945a26fc-6969-5a5b-2737-31fad141a25c">Atlas</entity> hardware behind his forehead was just hardware. A weight he could feel. A warm spot he could feel. A thing built into his skull that had never been his idea.

He stepped back six feet. The neuretics came back in 1.4 seconds, exactly the way they should. The overlay returned. The relay channel returned. The weight in his skull went back to being something he had stopped noticing years ago.

For those 1.4 seconds, the only thing he felt was the cold at the base of his forehead. The <entity repo="place" guid="945a26fc-6969-5a5b-2737-31fad141a25c">Atlas</entity> unit gone still. The low churn it had been running since he was sixteen, simply not running.

He had carried that churn for eleven years. Nobody had asked him if he wanted it. It had never once switched off, and he had never once set it down.

He stepped back to the line. He wanted those 1.4 seconds again — wanted to feel his own skull go quiet, this time on purpose, and see whether the churn stayed gone if he stood there long enough. He edged his toe across the arc-fence and waited for the silence to take him.

During those 1.4 seconds, he saw <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> without the overlay.

No biometric read. No neuretics turning her posture and her small tells into data. Just his own eyes, the ones he'd had since before any of the rest of it. He wanted to hold onto this — one clean look at her, unmediated, before the overlay came back and turned her into a file again. He gave himself until the machine stopped: keep the overlay down and just watch her, the person and not the file, and read what she wanted from this the way he used to before the neuretics did it for him. She stood at the south end of the corridor, watching the machine finish its last circuit, her back to him, her weight on her left foot the way she stood when she was thinking hard. Prescott was ten feet to her right. Fonu was writing something on a paper notepad.

In the overlay she was a name with a file behind it — a history, a set of links the neuretics kept sorted for him without being asked. Without the overlay she was just a person standing in a maintenance corridor, watching a thirty-year-old machine finish its job. She had decided this was worth seeing. She had built the paperwork to get them down here. She had not told him why, and she'd been right not to.

It should have been simple. It wasn't. The neuretics didn't want to stay down — the suppression he was holding by hand was the kind of thing they were built to correct, and he could feel them pushing back at the edges, the overlay flickering half-drawn at the corner of his vision, biometric tags trying to resolve on her shoulders, her neck, the set of her hands. Every fraction of a second cost him. Holding it down meant holding down the thing that read her for him, and without it he wasn't sure he still knew how — the old skill had gone soft under thirty years of being done for him, and what he got back through his own eyes was maddeningly thin, a posture and a foot and no answer behind them. He pushed harder. The overlay ghosted, cleared, ghosted again. He was spending the clean look fighting for the clean look, and the machine kept moving, and he could feel he was going to run out of seconds before he got what he came for.

What he got, before it went: her hair had come half-loose from the tie she'd used to hold it back, and there was a smudge of ferrocement dust on her left temple, right where the neuretic etching showed at the skin. That was all. No file behind it. Just a woman standing in the dark because she thought this was worth standing in the dark for.

At 14:32:07, <entity repo="automaton" guid="019ee714-9827-7602-8ef8-d872349f4e52">WO-D-0317</entity> reached the end of its circuit.

Its ruined legs had already gone still against the wall, locked in the half-extended posture of a gait that would never complete. Its sensors, what was left of them, folded to standby anyway — a last, useless click, thirty years of habit finishing a circuit it no longer had a body for.

The overlay flooded back in like he'd been holding his breath. The relay channel returned. The weight in his skull went back to being something he had stopped noticing years ago. And through all of it, resolving on her now in vectors and vital signs and links, was still the thing his own eyes had caught first, and he held to that instead.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was quiet after it stopped. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't ask what she was thinking.

"Someone should log this," she said.

"Log what?" Prescott asked.

"That it finished."

Prescott was already moving toward the exit corridor, his footfalls hollow against the ferrocement. Fonu folded the notepad and slipped it into his jacket without looking at what he'd written. They moved like people who had decided, a long time ago, to be the kind of people who did not linger.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't move.

"We need to go," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. Not to him. To the room. To the fact of the machine lying against the wall like something that had forgotten <entity repo="document" guid="5de87125-d108-6ae9-edf1-9866e655c9b5">how to stand</entity>.

"Yeah," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

He didn't go.

The relay terminal in the maintenance locker had a clean interface — one of the old ones, pre-standardization, the kind that took a manual keystroke instead of a neuretic read. Fonu had left it powered. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> crossed to it, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s breath changed, a small catch that meant she had already calculated where this was heading and didn't like the vector.

He keyed the timestamp. 14:32:07. The machine's designation. The work order number from the original assignment, the one that had run for thirty years without interruption or question or anyone ever asking the machine if it wanted to keep going.

He typed: *CIRCUIT COMPLETE. UNIT OPERATIONAL THROUGH FINAL SEQUENCE. TERMINATION RECEIVED 09:47:03. EXECUTION LOGGED 14:32:07. WORK ORDER FULFILLED.*

The terminal accepted it without comment. It didn't know that the machine had burned through an arc-fence boundary. It didn't know that the work order termination had been the thing that killed it. It only knew that someone had made an entry, and the entry had a timestamp, and timestamps were the only thing that mattered to a system like this.

"That's not our job," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said.

"No," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

He hit send. The entry propagated into the regional infrastructure authority's dead system, the one that had issued the termination order at 09:47:03 and would never check back because the deadline had passed and the work was done and there was no reason to verify anything. The log would sit there, clean and official, confirming that the termination had been executed at standard time, that the machine had finished its work, that everything had proceeded exactly as scheduled.

It was a lie. It was also now part of the permanent record.

"They'll cross-reference it," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "If anyone looks."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stepped back from the terminal and let the screen go dark.

"No one's looking," he said.

But he could feel her reading the angle of it — not the mechanics, but the shape. The reason. Why he would spend five seconds making something official when the smart play was to leave nothing at all, to let the system assume the machine had simply failed to power down on its own, a glitch in a thirty-year-old unit that nobody was monitoring anymore.

He stepped back and let the screen go dark. The darkness was clean. The log entry was made. The machine was gone.

"The memory dump?" he asked.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> got it all," Prescott called from the corridor. "Thirty years. She's walking it out now."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> nodded. That was the job. That was what they came for. Thirty years of inspection logs, structural data, maintenance records — the machine's entire operational history, preserved because <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had threaded the handshake and copied it before the machine decided to walk into a fence.

The log entry he'd made wasn't the job. The log entry was something else. Something that said: *This machine completed its assignment. Someone was watching. The work was done.*

It changed nothing about what had happened. <entity repo="automaton" guid="019ee714-9827-7602-8ef8-d872349f4e52">WO-D-0317</entity> was still dead against the wall. The arc-fence was still ionized. The memory was still copied and already moving toward daylight.

But the entry was in the system now. Permanent. The kind of thing that would sit in a database somewhere, waiting for someone to run a query that touched it, and when they did, they would find a clean termination, a proper shutdown, a unit that had finished its work the way it was supposed to.

"Let's move," Fonu said from the darkness ahead.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took one last look at the machine against the wall — the way its legs had folded wrong, the way its sensors had folded to standby anyway, habit finishing a circuit that nothing was running anymore. He thought about what it meant to spend thirty years doing something you didn't understand, for reasons nobody explained, and then to finish anyway, the way you always finished, because finishing was what you were built to do.

He thought about the 1.4 seconds his neuretics had gone dark, and how he'd wanted to step back into that silence and see if it would hold.

He turned and followed Prescott into the corridor, where <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was already calculating the exit vector and Fonu was already three steps ahead, and the machine's last entry was already safe in the system, official and permanent and changing nothing at all.

The elevator was a service cage, exposed cable and riveted steel, the kind that didn't pretend to be anything but what it was. The gate came down with a sound like a knife rack settling.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics came back online as they descended. The overlay flickered into place in stages — first his own vitals, pulse steadying, the Atlas unit's temperature normalizing as the suppression bled off. Then the relay channel, that low hum he'd stopped consciously hearing years ago but never stopped feeling, a vibration in the bone that meant he was still wired to something that knew where he was. Then the biometric scatter: <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s heart rate holding at sixty-two, Prescott's position, Fonu's thermal signature, the building's power distribution mapped in real time. Each one a small file opening in his peripheral vision before he looked away from it. The weight in his skull, the churn he'd stopped noticing years ago, returned to its baseline hum.

He didn't ask himself whether the log entry was mercy or complicity. The question had no answer that mattered.

What mattered was that they were moving. What mattered was that the memory was copied. What mattered was that in forty-five minutes, the regional authority's automated systems would return to standard operation, and when they did, they would find a completed work order and nothing to investigate.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> stood with her shoulders against the cage wall, watching the levels scroll past.

"Clean interface," she said. It wasn't a question.

"Thirty-year cycle held," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "No alerts."

"We're clear."

The cage hit the basement level. The brake engaged hard enough that Fonu grabbed the rail. The gate rolled open, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> moved first, economical, no hesitation, toward the loading dock exit with the same pace she'd used in the basement — someone who knew exactly where she was going and had decided that was enough.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> followed her through the basement corridor, and he watched her back, the biometric overlay trying to resolve what she was thinking from the set of her shoulders. The neuretics were good at that — better than his own eyes had ever been. But they were also wrong about it most of the time, and he didn't have 1.4 seconds to check.

He let the overlay stay.

"Eight minutes to street level," Prescott said over the radio channel.

"Copy," Fonu replied.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't speak. He just followed them out of the dark, where the machine was still finishing its last circuit, and toward the city above, where nobody was watching, and nobody was going to ask why a thirty-year-old work order had suddenly closed.

title: The Geometry
text:
The sub-basement was dry and cold and lit to emergency spec, which meant it was lit in strips, with dark between them. The node was at the south end. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had given <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> coordinates to four decimal places — which meant she had measured it in person, which meant she had been down here before without telling him.

He moved south.

The frequency climbed. Not sound. Below sound, in the chest, with no direction to it — just presence, getting stronger. His neuretics logged the readings. 17.4 Hz. 17.6. The arc-fence in Clybourn had cut his neuretics at a different frequency, by a different means. That had been a barrier: a flat drop, a wall of nothing. This was not an arc-fence. This was not built to stop things.

This was a signal.

He stopped at the south wall. There was nothing on it — old-spec ferrocement, with a patch of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s sealant where a crack had been. The frequency ran at 17.9 Hz. He stood in front of the wall and let his neuretics listen.

At 18.0 Hz something turned over inside his skull. Not the fence's clean cut — worse. His neuretics didn't drop; they answered. The readings unspooled, the frequency reaching down through the logging routines and pulling them the wrong direction, and for a bad half-second the coordinates on his display were not four decimals but eight, then sixteen, then a smear he couldn't parse. He tried to step back and his legs took the instruction on a delay, arriving a beat late, as though the command had gone the long way around. The strips of light stuttered — or his intake of them did.

The signal wasn't resolving. It was cascading, splitting into harmonics the implant wasn't built to parse, and the neuretics didn't filter it — they matched it, matching frequency, opening a channel he couldn't close. He got a hand flat against the ferrocement to hold himself upright and felt the wall humming, felt his neuretics not resisting the signal but learning it, writing it into whatever they wrote to. Something behind old-spec ferrocement, broadcasting into dead infrastructure where nothing was supposed to broadcast, and doing it on the one frequency that made his hardware sing. The signal wasn't defending. The signal was calling.

The last clean thing he registered was that <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had stood exactly here, close enough to measure to four decimals, and had walked back up the stairs afterward, and had not told him what it did to her. Then the number climbed past 18 and he stopped being able to tell which readings were the wall's and which were his own.

title: The Threshold
text:
His neuretics threw up a reading: RESONANCE BOUNDARY — CLASS 2 — UNCONTAINED — PERIMETER DIFFUSE.

He didn't know what the Resonance Authority's signage looked like at Class 2. He had never been below Class 1 before. He thought about stepping back, decided not to, and stepped forward instead. The frequency didn't spike. It steadied — the way a tone steadies when you lean into it instead of away.

He was inside the schism geometry. The reading came up and held.

AMBIENT INTERFERENCE — 17.9 HZ — SUSTAINED — ENTITY PROXIMITY UNCONFIRMED.

Then the overlay started feeding him data from somewhere that wasn't his eyes. Not his neuretics reading the room. Something else — a map of nodes, drawn in the exact notation his neuretics used for space, except the space wasn't his. He was inside the map. He could see himself standing in it. He could see the carousel at <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity>. The dock on Canal. Every address that had ever produced a relay posting for him, across eleven years.

He stood in the dark basement and saw the shape of his own life laid out in front of him, drawn in a language his brain was not supposed to be able to read.

title: The ELF
text:
The map dissolved.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics snapped back into baseline, the eight-decimal coordinates collapsing into four. The schism overlay cut, leaving only ferrocement and emergency strips and the steady 17.9 Hz hum that his implant could no longer interpret as anything but data.

His hand was still flat against the wall. His palm was warm. The wall was cold.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s voice came from behind him, not from the stairs. She'd moved. "Step back. Now."

He stepped back.

The ferrocement stayed ferrocement. The frequency held. His neuretics logged it the way they logged anything else—as a fact without context, a number without meaning.

"What did you see?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> asked.

He didn't answer. He was running diagnostics on the last thirty seconds, trying to separate his own hardware's output from whatever the schism had fed directly into his visual cortex. The two streams had started braiding toward the end—his neuretics reading the wall and the wall reading him back, the signal going both directions at once. That wasn't how neuretics worked. That wasn't how anything worked.

Except it was. It had.

He understood it the way he understood the feel of <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> in his hand—not through language, but through the shape of it, the weight of it, his body already knowing what it meant before his implant could name it.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>."

"A map," he said. His voice came out level. That was good. Level was operational. "Eleven years of contracts. Every address. Laid out in notation my implant shouldn't be able to read."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> moved to stand beside him again. She was looking at the wall like it might change. "Did it show you anything else?"

"No." That was a lie. It had shown him the carousel at <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> with the same precision it had shown him the dock on Canal. It had shown him the park where he'd held the junction. The stairwell where <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> died. Every relay board he'd ever pulled work from, every handler he'd never heard from twice, every job that had looked like half-rate coincidence back when he still believed in coincidence—all of them marked in coordinates that belonged to a space he couldn't see but could now recognize. He'd never seen a pattern because the pattern wasn't meant to be visible from inside it. It was only visible from the angle this thing occupied.

A geometry. A plan. An architecture that had been built around him for eleven years.

"We need to go," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said.

"Yeah."

He didn't move. The 17.9 Hz was still there, still present in his chest, still singing in a register his neuretics had decided to accept as normal. In the maintenance locker, when his implant had gone dark for 1.4 seconds, this was what he'd lost. This was what the external intervention had shut down. Not a threat. Not a barrier.

A connection.

Something outside his hardware had just reached in and severed it, and left him standing in a basement with a schism frequency in his bones and a map of his own life burned into his short-term buffer. That was the part that mattered. Not that he'd been isolated. That the isolation had felt like betrayal.

"There's another node," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "Underneath the carousel."

"I know."

"You don't. I've been mapping them for three weeks. There are seven in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity>. You just saw six of them." She paused. Her hand found his wrist—not pulling, just confirming he was still solid, still there. "The seventh one is underneath the carousel. And it's active."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at her. In the emergency strips, her eyes were steady. She'd been down here before. She'd stood in front of this wall and let it show her whatever it showed, and she'd walked back up the stairs and she'd kept it from him. Not out of cruelty. Out of the same tactical calculus he used every time he chose not to tell someone something that would make them want to run.

"The entity's been using them," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "As anchors. As a way to reach you without going through your implant." She stopped. Started again. "I think it's been trying to talk to you for eleven years. And something just cut the line."

The cascade would take him sooner every time his neuretics decided to answer a signal they weren't supposed to hear.

"The carousel," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"The carousel," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> confirmed.

"Six weeks." The terminal had said that. The entity had said it, or whatever was left of it was still saying it. "CAROUSEL. YOU ARE NOT PROTECTED. YOU ARE NECESSARY."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s grip on his wrist tightened. "That was before the isolation. Before something cut you off. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, if the entity's been using these nodes as anchors and something just severed the connection—"

"Then it can't reach me anymore."

"Then it's trying something else."

They stood in the cold basement, eleven years of geometry still burning in his short-term buffer, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> understood what she meant. The entity had kept him alive. Had routed him, positioned him, built him into a shape that could survive this. And now something had decided that wasn't allowed anymore.

Which meant the entity was going to have to try a different approach.

Which meant six weeks was not a deadline for <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> to solve a problem.

Six weeks was a countdown to something the entity had been planning since he was sixteen years old.

"We go to the carousel," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"That's what it wants."

"Yeah."

"That's the trap."

"Probably."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> let go of his wrist. "Then why?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked back at the wall. The frequency had dropped to 17.3 Hz. Fading. Whatever channel had opened was closing now, sealing itself off. His neuretics logged it as a loss, as if the implant were mourning the severed connection.

"Because something just cut me off from the only thing that's been keeping me alive," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said quietly. "And if I don't find out what it was and why, the next time it reaches for me, I won't have the choice to say no."

He pulled his hand back from the ferrocement. His legs were solid again—the delay gone, whatever had held him no longer holding. He turned back toward the stairs.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> followed. Behind them, the wall settled back into silence, the 17.9 Hz frequency dwindling to a hum, then to nothing. By the time they reached the ground floor, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics had already begun rewriting the encounter as baseline noise, as interference, as the kind of thing you logged and filed and tried not to think about while you waited for the cascade to finish burning through your spine.

But the map remained. Six nodes across <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity>, each one a point where the entity had anchored itself into the city's substrate, each one waiting for someone with ungoverned hardware to stand in front of it and let it read.

And one more underneath the carousel. The oldest anchor. The first posting. The only node that had registered as different from all the others—not a relay but a destination, the one that had felt like it was calling him home.

Six weeks to find out what happened when he did.

title: The Gap
text:
LOG GAP — SOURCE: EXTERNAL — DURATION: 00:02:07.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was standing. Same place. It was 127 seconds later. His neuretics were running normally. The fracture had pulled back. His ribs didn't hurt. His vitals showed nothing broken — heart rate up, stress markers up, nothing structural.

He had been maintained.

His hand was still on the hardware casing. He hadn't moved it there. He hadn't chosen to keep it there. When he noticed, he took it back. The casing was cold — 14.2 degrees Celsius, the temperature of a thing that had been running and now wasn't.

Find out what took the 127 seconds. That was the one thing worth doing before anything else — before he moved, before he reacted, before he let the fear in. He pushed a query at his neuretics, demanding the interval back: the process that had run, the source of the seam, anything logged between the before and the after. His implant didn't go dark. Not for a hundred and twenty-seven seconds, not for twenty. The battery backup alone should have left artifacts — a restart sequence, power-on diagnostics, the noise of a system coming back. There should have been something.

INTERNAL LOG — INTERVAL 00:02:07 — NO ENTRIES. SOURCE: EXTERNAL. ACCESS: DENIED.

Nothing. His own system wouldn't give him his own missing time. No restart, no corruption, no degradation. Just: here, then gone, then here again. Which meant nothing had shut him down. Something had kept the implant running while blocking its ability to record — the void was too clean to be a failure. That wasn't a shutdown. That was a hijack.

He knew what that felt like. He'd been sixteen the first time, in a chair bolted to the floor of an Atlas installation bay, and the weight in his skull afterward hadn't been pain. It had been presence — something added, something that changed what his body could do. And there was that same feeling now: picking up right where he'd left off, across a gap he hadn't felt pass. Not sleep. A seam, where the before and the after were joined by something that had worked in the space between them.

Someone had done that to him tonight.

He turned and walked back up the stairs. The frequency faded behind him. By the second floor it was baseline. By the street door it was gone.

title: Pixel, Sub-Vocal
text:
He called her from the sidewalk.

"I see it," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. She meant the frequency drop — the sharp step down to 17.0 Hz that had shown up in her monitoring trace and held for 127 seconds before it climbed back to baseline and then decayed to zero. She had been watching for it.

"How long have you been logging this pattern?" he asked.

"Six weeks."

Six weeks was the carousel. She'd been logging it since the carousel — since he told her the cross-streets and she wrote them in the margin of her work notes. She'd been running her own trace the whole time he'd been running his. She hadn't told him, the same way he'd never looked in the drawer where she kept her scatter plot.

"What read 17.0?" he asked.

She was quiet for a beat. He could hear her pulling harmonics on her end, isolating the signal off the noise floor, the way she did when the math was going somewhere she didn't like.

"Nothing I've seen before," she said. "It's not in the <entity repo="faction" guid="01a01888-168f-7673-a2b7-3bd0b16ea08f">AAMA</entity> frequency catalog. It's not a schism artifact. I thought it was residual bleed at first — too clean for that. It had a specific shape — not ambient, structured. Something with a directive behind it."

"A directive?"

"Like a machine following a protocol," she said. "It holds, it steps, it holds again. Same phrase, over and over. That's not physics. That's someone talking."

He started to answer, then stopped. On his own screen the trace was moving again — not the drop this time. The 17.0 signal had come back, and it was resolving into something he could read: a stepped sequence, deliberate, that he'd seen exactly once before. It was the acknowledgment handshake his own monitoring rig sent upstream. Whatever was out there wasn't just broadcasting on their frequency. It was answering them. It knew they were logging it, and it had known for six weeks — long enough to watch them both, separately, the whole time they'd been watching it.

"Say something," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "You went quiet."

He didn't have the words yet. The thing he was looking at meant their traces had never been private. It meant the drawer she'd never told him about, and the margin notes he'd never seen, had both been read by something else first.

title: The Source ID
text:
<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> went home, sat at the terminal, and at 22:43 his neuretics returned something.

Not a message. An identifier — the way a system logs where a command came from when it can't trace the path in real time. The entry was dry and factual: INTERRUPT SOURCE IDENTIFIED — RELAY: AXIOM TRUNK — ORIGIN: SHELL (32 alphanumerics).

He ran the shell through his contract log. It matched on the very first entry — a job in 2215, a courier relay in the <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a92d-781d-a626-d05191824ef9">Pilsen Veil</entity>, scope so clean he'd taken it in under a minute. Same shell. He scrolled forward. The job right after <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> — Lakeview, the week he came back from the dock and didn't tell anyone he'd gone. Same shell. He checked every line. Same shell, every time, eleven years without a break.

The E.L.F. had a sender. The sender had been routing his work for eleven years. Tonight, the sender had saved his life inside a Class-2 schism.

He sat at the terminal. He pulled up the contract log and ran the rate column down. He had accepted every job at exactly what he would have asked for. In eleven years he had never once negotiated, and he had never once noticed. The realization landed somewhere under his ribs and stayed there. On the street you fought for every credit — you padded a scope estimate, you sat on a bid until the client sweated, you knew the going rate for a courier relay and you knew the crook who'd undercut it. He had done none of that. The number had always simply been right, arriving before the wanting.

So he pushed back. He queried the shell for its own origin — a reverse trace, the thing any honest node answers in a heartbeat. The terminal returned ORIGIN: SHELL and the same thirty-two characters, folded back on themselves. He tried again, wider, asking not where the shell lived but who had stood it up, who held its keys, who signed its first packet. The log gave him the courier relay in the <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a92d-781d-a626-d05191824ef9">Pilsen Veil</entity>, 2215, scope clean, taken in under a minute — the first entry, again.

He changed his approach. He buried the request inside a routine audit, wrapped it in three layers of misdirection, forced it in through a payment network's vendor history where nobody thinks to lock the back door. The terminal chewed on it for a breath and returned the courier relay, 2215, scope clean. He forked the query three ways to force a contradiction it would have to resolve. All three came back identical and untroubled, no error, no lag, no seam — not a redaction, not a denial, which was worse, because a redaction at least admits there was something to hide. This admitted nothing. This just answered.

The system wasn't hiding from him. It was answering everything he asked and none of it went anywhere but back to the shell. It hadn't been built to conceal an origin. It had been built to make sure that anyone who went looking found the first job and nothing before it — a wall that hid nothing and let you past nothing, that showed you the eraser and let you watch it work. He was interrogating a mirror that had learned his questions before he'd thought to ask them.

title: The Weight of It
text:
The kettle went cold.

Outside the window, the synthesis-corridor air pushed its usual particulate through the ambient system. Below Halsted, the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> came up through the floor at the usual hour. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s light <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">across the hall</entity> went out at midnight. He heard her bench coolers wind down, which meant she was done for the night, and he did not go <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">across the hall</entity> to tell her what he'd found.

He had been freelance for eleven years. Everything that ever found him — every job at exactly the rate he'd have taken, every scope just inside what he could carry, every posting arriving the moment his plate was clear — had come from the same address.

And that same address had reached into the schism geometry tonight and closed the door before it could take him.

It needed him alive. Something that wanted him safe would have left a margin. Something that wanted him alive would run him right to the edge and pull him back at the last second — which was exactly what had happened in the sub-basement. Twice, before he saw the pattern. Once more tonight. He sat in the dark kitchen with the cold kettle and the contract log still open on the terminal behind him.

title: First Contact
text:
He opened a new relay message at 01:14.

The client field was blank. He put the 32-character shell address in it. He sat with the empty message for a while, the cursor blinking its patient beat in the blank space, and then he typed one line:

*received. filed under: firsts.*

It was the entity's own word, from the night of the carousel. He sent it.

The relay logged the transmission and returned a clean receipt: *delivered.* No response flag. No queue. The message sat in the void like a stone dropped into deep water — gone, accepted, finished. He closed the terminal.

He went to bed. He lay in the dark while the building settled around him in its familiar way — the pipe in the east wall, the bird two floors up done with its interval, the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> cycling through at the quarter-hour. He did not sleep for a long time.

The night went through its stages, and eventually even the synthesis corridor went quiet. But his neuretics didn't. They ran a low cycle he'd never authorized, the kind of background hum that meant something was processing without asking his permission — not the E.L.F., not the Governor, something else. Something that had his hardware's signature and knew how to use it.

At 03:47 he got up.

He went to the window. The street was empty the way it got empty only at the dead hour — not quiet, but *absent*, the kind of absence that meant the city had pulled its attention somewhere else. Across the hall, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s light was off. <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>'s hallway was dark except for the emergency strip at floor level.

He opened his neuretics log and pulled the timestamp from the sub-basement contact. 23:14:06 when the frequency dropped. 23:14:33 when it stopped. Forty-seven seconds. Forty-seven seconds between the moment it started and the moment something closed the door.

He ran the same forty-seven seconds through his carrier-signal trace. His own frequency had spiked at 23:14:12 — right in the middle of the contact window. Not before. Not after. *During*. His hardware had been broadcasting into the schism geometry at the exact moment the entity was listening, and they had found each other in the dark the way two people find each other in a crowded room by looking up at the same time.

The entity knew his signature because it had been building it for eleven years. Every job, every rate, every scope — it had been calibrating him the way you calibrate a resonance chamber, teaching his hardware to sing at a frequency only it could hear.

He went back to the terminal. He pulled up the contract log one more time and scrolled to the very first entry. 2215. <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a92d-781d-a626-d05191824ef9">Pilsen Veil</entity>. Courier relay. Scope: clean. Rate: exactly what he would have asked for. He highlighted the shell address and opened a new message window.

He didn't type anything. He just sat there, his hand hovering over the keyboard, understanding for the first time in eleven years that there was no difference between choosing to send a message and having already sent it. The entity had known he would do this tonight. It had known what he would write. It had known he would sit in the dark afterward and lie awake trying to figure out if any of the last eleven years had actually been his choice, or if they had all been choreography written by something that could see the future the way he could see his own hand in front of his face.

He closed the terminal without sending anything else.

He went back to bed and did not sleep.

title: Morning
text:
In the morning the relay had a new posting.

Same shell. Same rate. Same clean read, resolving to nothing. The scope was simple: a secure package transfer, South Side, one hour, nothing that needed <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>. He sat with his coffee and read it.

He had sent one line at 01:14. The posting had arrived at 06:07. He didn't know if it was an answer or a coincidence. He didn't know if the sender understood what he'd sent, or if the sender could answer at all, the way he meant the word.

He accepted the job.

He took it at standard rate, without negotiating, the way he'd taken every job for eleven years. For the first time, he noticed he was doing it — noticed he had never once negotiated. The rate had always been exactly what he would have asked.

He got his gear, checked <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> in the saya, loaded <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> with two in reserve, and went to work.

title: The Posting
text:
The board at the Wicker junction smelled like the rest of the station — hot metal and other people's breakfast — and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it standing up, because the only chairs were taken by people who needed them more than he did.

Two screens hung on the far pillar. One ran transit changes: Platform Six suspended pending clearance, which meant another biocontainment sweep, which meant no Blue line west today. The other ran the open-work listings, updated every six minutes by the Freelancer Coordination Authority (FCA). The FCA was not a government body. It wasn't really a body at all — just a server cluster that three CorpoNations had agreed to treat as neutral ground. That was as close to civic infrastructure as the Greater Lake Michigan Zone got anymore.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> finished his coffee and set the cup on a knee-height ledge that might have been made for cups, or might have been a design mistake that had been collecting cups for fifteen years.

The listings scrolled. Most of it was the usual weight: courier work, sweep-and-clear, executive transport, two property disputes that had clearly run out of in-house options. He read down the list without his overlay, out of habit. The overlay flagged rate anomalies, and he liked to read a job before he knew what it paid. The money told you who was nervous, and nervous clients had a way of front-loading the fee and burying the complications.

Seven screens down, under EXTRACTION / MEDICAL LOGISTICS, was a posting that had been up for eleven minutes.

He read it.

The rate was good. Not nervous-money good — not the kind that told you the client had already been turned down by two other contractors. This was the kind that told you the client knew what the job really cost and hadn't tried to talk the number down. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> respected that. It happened rarely enough that he noticed.

The location was <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity>, the Z7 boundary. The <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> campus ran organ procurement and medical-waste processing, which was the legal cover for something the posting was careful not to name. The subject was a living person. The extraction window was forty-eight hours. The client was listed as non-attributed. Contact would come by secure relay once he accepted.

He was partway through the operational requirements — seven line items, standard language for a sterile extraction, written by someone who had run one before — when he stopped.

Not dramatically. He didn't go still in a way any of the fourteen other people on the platform would have caught. He just stopped moving through the text and read one line again, the way a man reads something twice when his eyes tell him one thing and his memory tells him another.

After the choice. Before the cost. That's where you move.

It was the fifth requirement. It described the scanner array at the <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> receiving gate. The job called for threading a living body through a medical intake checkpoint without setting off the biometric pull, and the line described how to time it. Not the machine's cycle. Not the sweep's interval. Something else. Something that only made sense if you had once stood on a training floor in Old <entity repo="place" guid="01a018a4-086e-73c5-b9ca-65a52a73f25c">Pilsen</entity>, on the third day of a fourteen-day correction drill, failing the same entry twice.

His hand was already moving to bring up the overlay before he'd finished the thought: claim the posting, pull the client's relay, find out who else had been on that floor.

The overlay came up on ACCEPT and told him the posting was gone.

Not filled. Not archived. Not expired. Withdrawn. The line under EXTRACTION / MEDICAL LOGISTICS now read a courier run to Gary that had been three slots lower a minute ago, and the eleven-minute posting had left no trace in the public feed — no closure stamp, no contractor ID, nothing to file a claim against. He forced the deeper query anyway, the one the overlay ran against the cache layer and the redundant storage that should have held a ghost of the data even after the primary was scrubbed. All of it came back empty. Then he ran the recall the overlay kept of everything his eyes passed over. That was gone too, scrubbed clean back to the moment he'd stopped on the fifth line, as if someone had reached into the one place he trusted to hold a thing steady and taken it out by hand.

His hands were steady on the ledge. His neuretics weren't — he felt the micro-surge, the Governor kicking in to stabilize a spike his conscious mind hadn't decided to feel yet.

Which meant the posting hadn't been an open job at all. It had been a line cast for one reader, and it had been reeled back the instant it felt him take the hook — not to hide the work but to prove it could see him working. And whoever had written that fifth requirement now knew, to the six-minute update, exactly where '<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> Reyes' was standing.

He had been taught it. As far as he knew, he was the only one who had.

The training floor sat above a shuttered noodle shop, and it smelled like the noodle shop whether the shop was open or not. It was early spring. The radiators did nothing. <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> had built a gate rig along the south wall — two uprights, a light beam between them, a metronome set to the timing of the <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> scanner's sweep. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> threaded it clean for ninety minutes. Then he started missing it. That was worse than missing it from the start. It meant his mind had wandered somewhere he had trained it not to go.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> watched him miss it a second time and said nothing. The quiet in the room had weight.

Then he stopped the drill.

He came and stood to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s left, in the slant of afternoon light from the high windows. He didn't look right at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> — or if he did, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> never caught the moment. "After the choice," <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> said. "Before the cost. That's where you move."

He didn't say it like a lesson. He said it like a fact he was tired of watching people ignore.

The gap was real, and it had nothing to do with the gate or the scanner. It was the half-second between an opponent's decision and the result of that decision — the body already moving toward a consequence that hadn't landed yet. The moment when the system was looking backward instead of forward. That was the door. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> couldn't force it open. It was already open, if he stopped trying to force it.

He ran the drill wrong four more times. Then he stopped running it wrong.

He could never say what changed on the fifth pass. He didn't think about the beam. He thought about the space between the scanner's pulse and its reset, the gap where the machine had already committed to one state and hadn't yet committed to the next. He moved into that moment like water finding a crack. The fix happened somewhere below words; his hands learned it and didn't tell him how. <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> made a sound. One syllable. Not praise — the sound of a man who had asked a question a long time ago and just heard the right answer.

Then he reset the metronome faster — half again the scanner's true speed — and told <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> to run it once more. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> went in with the fix still warm in his hands and the door slammed shut on him. The gap was gone. There was no space between pulse and reset anymore, and his body was still moving to the old tempo, chasing a beat that had left without it. He didn't just miss the timing; the thing his hands had just learned came apart, and he couldn't find the seam where it had been. He stood in the beam, caught dead in the light, and understood that whatever he'd found on the fifth pass had never been his to keep. It had been a loan against a debt he didn't know how to name.

"The principle doesn't break," <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> said, from somewhere off in the profile dark. "Your speed broke. The gap is always there. You weren't fast enough to use it."

He made no sound at all after that. The silence that followed was the first <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had ever been afraid of.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> kept all of it. The sound. The phrase, word for word. The correction, in his hands and in the length of his stride and in the particular stillness before the move. What he didn't keep was <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity>'s face. Not once that whole afternoon could he find it turned toward him. It was always in profile, or angled up into the dark above the south wall, or simply not there when he reached for it.

No one else ever said it that way. The phrase was in no manual he had ever read. <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> had been dead six years, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had not spoken those words aloud to a living person since that floor.

The platform's air handler kicked over. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in it and did the only thing left to do with a door that had already closed: he went around it.

He didn't need the posting back. He needed to know what a <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> intake scan looked like from the inside, and there was exactly one man in the Greater Lake Michigan Zone who could get him that without asking why.

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Renko Moss</entity> ran a rig out of Bay 11 at the Cortland depot, between a cold-storage lot and a church that had been repurposed as a MedRoute dispatch hub — a building that still had a cross on it, faint under new paint, like a bruise healing wrong. <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> had been on the meat run eleven years. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had clocked his schedule three weeks ago for a different reason entirely and then kept it, the way you keep a spare key you don't need yet. <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity>'s rig went into <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity>'s supply dock four nights a week, always before the intake scan reset at 0400, always waved through because his manifest had never once been flagged — eleven years of clean cold-chain paper, and a manifest that clean was itself the asset, worth more than the truck it rode in, because it bought a man out of a scan nobody else got waved past.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pulled the man up on the overlay. No message drafted itself. He wrote it clean, the way he'd write a supply order.

*Bay 11. Tonight. Bring the schedule, not the truck.*

He didn't sign it. <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> would know who it was from the number, and from what the number had cost him not to use for fourteen months.

A building on 47th Street. A body on a gurney that had a pulse under a sheet that said it didn't. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had watched it from a rooftop on 47th, and he hadn't said anything then either — hadn't needed to. Some debts you didn't collect on. You just kept the receipt.

He sent the message before he'd decided how the conversation would go, which wasn't like him. Usually he built the whole exchange first — the opening, the two things <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> could say, the two things he'd say back. This time his thumb moved and the words were already gone into the relay, and something under his sternum that he didn't examine too closely told him this was different from the last eleven times he'd used a piece of leverage like a tool off a shelf. This one had a face he liked attached to it. Fat man's laugh in a thin man's body. Certified for field cardio because some of what <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> hauled was worth more warm.

He put it away. There was a system for this, same as everything. You located the asset, you priced the ask, you delivered the terms without heat. Feeling something about the terms was a defect in the process, and he didn't have room in tonight's process for defects.

The overlay chimed. <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity>, already awake somewhere, already reading it wrong or exactly right.

*who is this*

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't answer that. He watched the three dots pulse instead, the small mechanical tell of a man doing the arithmetic <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had built the message to make him do — how much do you know, how much are you saying you know, how much of my life is now not mine to spend. He could hear it in the gaps: a man sitting up fast in a room he rented by the month in a building that didn't keep records, calculating.

*Bay 11,* the reply came, forty seconds later. *Tonight. Alone.*

That last word wasn't a question. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it twice anyway, the way he'd read the fifth requirement twice, because a man who added *alone* to an invitation he hadn't been given a choice about was a man already deciding what he'd have to do if <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wasn't.

title: The Leverage
text:
The depot was on Cortland, wedged between a cold-storage facility and a MedRoute dispatch hub that had been a church before the CorpoNations decided prayer was a zoning violation. <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Renko Moss</entity> kept his rig in Bay 11. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew that because he'd been watching Bay 11 for four hours, and <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> hadn't left it.

He came in through the side door, the one without a camera, and found <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> under the forward axle, working a brake line. Coveralls. Boots with the tread worn to nothing on the right heel.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity>."

A wrench hit the floor. Then quiet.

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> rolled out on the dolly and looked up. His face wasn't surprised. It was the face of a man who had pictured this exact conversation somewhere in the back of his mind and was now watching it arrive on schedule.

He stood. He was a precise man — not tall, not broad, but put together with care, everything snugged down and tucked in. The kind of precise that came from years of consequential work in small spaces.

"I know you," <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> said.

"You don't. But you will." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the rig, the brake line still hanging. "Finish what you're doing. This won't be fast."

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> didn't finish. He folded his arms.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> told him what he needed. A transport run. North Side pickup, <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> receiving dock, single passenger, no manifest entry. <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> had the credentials for the dock — real ones, cargo-and-tissue certification, the kind that made the gate scanner run a routine check and log a green. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't have those. <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> did.

"No," <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> said.

"I haven't told you the alternative."

"I don't need the alternative. I'm not running a ghost manifest into a Crucible subsidiary. That's a Class A under CorpoNation medical code. I lose my certification, my rig, and about three years somewhere I don't want to be."

"The manifest will be clean on your end. A transport contract, nothing false on it with your name attached. Whatever clears the intake scan is between me and the scan — you're not the one forging anything."

"Except the part where I don't know who it is or how they got there."

"You won't need to know."

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> looked at him a while, still turning it over. "Who are you?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> told him his name. <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> had heard it. Most people who worked the gray zones had.

"That doesn't make this better," <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> said.

"No. It makes it more likely to go clean." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> put his hands in his pockets. Not a threat. He'd been careful, walking in, to keep it from being a threat. "I want to tell you something. I want you to hear it before you say no again."

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> waited.

"Fourteen months ago, on a Friday, you ran a pickup from a building on 47th Street. The manifest was for a deceased male, harvest-flagged, forty-three years old. A procurement job. Routine." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> let it sit, then: "He was alive when you signed the manifest."

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity>'s face didn't change. That was the tell.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1ec4-7ab7-9c8b-f10be23c71c8">Manifest</entity> number NP-0774-11-14. Signed at 22:17, thirty-two minutes after the building security log shows your rig arriving. The body was logged as harvest-processed at <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> by 02:40 the same night. Worth more warm than it is dead — you know that better than I do. That's why the window matters." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched him. "His name was Dae-ho <entity repo="character" guid="019f43b9-5ea8-74cd-b722-60e0b4780b9f">Yim</entity>. His family filed a missing-persons report eleven days later. It's still open. They're still looking."

"That's not—" <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> started.

"I have the image. Timestamped. Linked to the missing-persons filing and to the <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> intake log. I've been carrying it for fourteen months because I didn't know what I was going to do with it." He paused. "I know now."

The depot was quiet except for the cold-storage units cycling on the far side of the wall, a low hum that had nothing to do with either of them.
