"If you say no," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, "I'm not going to publish it. I want that clear. I'm not here to destroy you. You made a bad call, in a city that makes bad calls easy and then makes you live on them, and you've carried it for over a year. I'm not your confessor. I'm just the man who saw it." He met <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity>'s eyes. "If you say no, I find another route. I lose time. The one I'm trying to get out might not have the time to spare — but that's my problem, not yours. You walk away and I never come back."

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> said nothing.

"If you say yes, we run the job, the patient gets out, and you get paid. Standard rate for a certified medical transport. All above the table. When it's done, the image stays in my overlay and you never hear from me again. That's the whole offer."

"You're asking me to trust that."

"No. I'm asking you to weigh it." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the hanging brake line. "You're a precise man. You already know what it comes to."

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> turned away. He walked to the front of the rig and put both hands flat on the hood, not leaning, just standing there. The cold-storage units cycled again.

When he turned back, his face was different. Not settled, exactly. More like a man who had argued himself out of it and lost.

"When?" he asked.

"Thursday. 23:00."

"I want the rate upfront."

"Half upfront. Half when the patient's in the vehicle."

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> considered it. His jaw worked once, like he was chewing something that tasted bad. Then he nodded — the nod of a man who'd already lost an argument he'd started with himself.

"Bay 11," he said. "23:00. Don't be late."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said he wouldn't be. He left through the same side door, into the cold North Side night, and didn't look back at the church that wasn't a church anymore.

title: The Night Before
text:
The form had a principle, not a name. <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> had named it once, but <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> no longer had the name — it had gone the way you lose a word, not in a moment but in the slow absence of any reason to use it. What stayed was the principle: after the choice, before the cost. The half-second between them, where the body finishes what the mind already chose. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had spent eleven days trying to make that half-second stop being something he had to think about.

His hands had it now. His hands had had it for years.

He ran the form in the narrow space between the cot and the window, <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> in his right hand, the city's low orange light lying across the floor. The blade came out of the saya without sound — matte composite, steel-CNT, the weight exactly where it should be. Third correction: the elbow drops first, then the lead hand turns at full extension, a half-turn that takes the steel from diagonal to true horizontal — a small move the muscles had to learn the way water learns a drain.

The form turned. His lead hand rotated. The steel crossed horizontal and the light ran off <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> and along the back wall, a half-second stripe.

Clean. The way it was meant to be.

He ran it again.

What he couldn't find was the afternoon. He knew it had been afternoon — the light in the memory was slanted and warm, a west-facing room, late. He knew <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> had watched him run it wrong ten times and said nothing, the patient kind of teaching that had made <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> angrier than being corrected would have.

He had the words in <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity>'s voice — the flatness of them, said once and never repeated, as if repeating a thing were a kind of doubt <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> didn't carry. *Precision lives in the millimeter,* <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> had said. *Everywhere else is approximation.* He had the words and not the room they were said in. He didn't have the face.

He had the pride of it — a tightness across his sternum that his neuretics read back to him as recognition, positive. The feeling was there. The scene it belonged to had edges but nothing inside them.

He ran the form a third time.

The NeoCortex overlay was quiet tonight, running background ambient — door locked, temperature fine, the street below cycling through the ordinary sounds of Z5 at 0100: three restaurant exhaust fans, a truck idling two blocks north, someone moving fast on foot through an alley, nothing flagged hostile. The overlay never fully shut off. He'd stopped noticing it the way you stop noticing your own pulse.

On the fourth pass his lead hand did something slightly off — a tenth of a degree in the turn, nothing anyone watching would have caught — and his body corrected it before the thought arrived. The fix came from somewhere below the NeoCortex, from whatever underlay the composite or was part of it or had long since become the same thing. Something down there had held a blade before. Probably more than one. The blade moved like it was following a groove worn into the world long before his body learned to walk it.

He didn't dwell on it. He thought about the form.

The tightness across his sternum was still there, faint now. <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> had looked at him. The light had been western. The room had a floor and a quiet and a temperature he couldn't get back. What he had was the shape of the moment, and the shape was enough to run the form by. The man who trained his hands had left the training and not the man.

He'd eaten two hours ago: rice, tinned protein, something pickled that <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> had pressed into his hand without pricing it — which meant it was yesterday's batch, which meant she trusted him not to complain. He'd left Φ20 on the counter, five more than the meal was worth. She'd read it as credit against vegetables to come. For three years they'd settled up to the exact coin.

His weapons lay on the cot behind him in the order he'd put them on: <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> on the left, sheathed for the night, cylinder loaded, two spare loads in the case beside it. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> in his hand for now. Tomorrow he'd go left-side first, then right. The brief said confined spaces and a man he'd need leverage over — the kind of work where drawing slow beat drawing fast, where the sword was the last option and so the useful one.

He ran the form a last time.

The half-turn at full extension. The steel through horizontal — and this time the tightness across his sternum pulled, not faint, a hard hook under the breastbone, and his hand faltered on the horizontal. Not the tenth-of-a-degree slip the body fixed on its own. This one his body didn't fix, because it wasn't in the hand. It was in the wanting to see the room again, the wanting rising unbidden the way it hadn't in years, and the wanting turned <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> a fraction and stole the half-second clean. He tried to run through it and the memory closed its edges tighter the harder he pushed, a door that shut faster the more weight he put against it. The neuretics flagged the spike — recognition, negative — and he stood there in the orange light with <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> wrong in his hand and the room he couldn't enter no closer than it had ever been, and something in his chest that wanted it anyway, refusing, after all these years, to let it stay a settled thing. The stripe of light crossed the wall and stopped in the wrong place.

He'd stopped trying, years ago, to find the afternoon. It had stopped being a question. It was just there — a gap in the map, a room he couldn't enter, a face he could hold still only from the one angle that left out the moment of being seen.

He had the form. The form was real. The form knew exactly what it was for.

He sheathed <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> — <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> home in the saya, giving the light nothing back.

Tomorrow was a body farm on the north end, a transport driver with a paperwork problem, and a researcher someone had decided not to waste. The brief was clean. The hook in it had been the phrase, word for word. He'd chosen not to look too hard at that. Looking wouldn't help at 0100. Tomorrow was a job.

He was ready. He lay down on the cot, weapons beside him in their order, and the city's low orange came through the window, and he was asleep before the NeoCortex finished its end-of-waking check.

title: The Transport
text:
The bus was already rolling north when <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> taped the second lead down. He pressed harder than he needed to. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt it.

"Core temp needs to read forty-eight Fahrenheit by the time we hit the dock," <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> said. He wasn't looking at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. He was watching the readout on the portable monitor clamped to the gurney rail, reading the line of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s vitals like bad news he'd written himself. "<entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> intake scans core temp, pulse, and the death cert on the slate. It doesn't read carefully. Nobody breaks into a body farm."

"No one but me."

"You'll have four hours before the cooler rotation. After that you're inventory." <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> pulled the cooling blanket up over <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s chest with two sharp tugs. "Inventory gets opened."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> lay still. The contact gel was cold enough to feel through the leads, a wet chill spreading out from each electrode. Outside, the city came up through the floor — the particular judder of northside asphalt, potholed and patched in a pattern <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew without naming it.

Fourteen months ago he'd been on a rooftop on 47th, working a different job, and had watched <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> come out the back of the bus below and sign a living man as deceased on the delivery manifest. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had kept the image — sealed, labeled, available. He'd pulled it out when <entity repo="character" guid="019dd276-fb32-7130-bba7-08604333865f">Hua</entity> handed him this contract and said there was only one crew chief on the North Side who'd run this route.

The conversation after that had been short.

"Your hardware," <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> said now. He stopped. He set down the tape. He looked at the monitor, then at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. His face did the thing <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had seen it do twice before — something between disgust and a cost he resented paying. "It does — whatever it does?"

"In theory."

"In theory?" The word came out flat and contaminated. <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity>'s jaw worked once. "<entity repo="place" guid="945a26fc-6969-5a5b-2737-31fad141a25c">Atlas</entity>-grade NeoCortex in a field-temp drop. Theory. The last confirmed <entity repo="place" guid="945a26fc-6969-5a5b-2737-31fad141a25c">Atlas</entity> installation was a corpo lab with a dedicated resuscitation team and two surgeons on standby."

"Three surgeons," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "The third was backup."

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> looked at him.

"I read the file," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"The file is classified."

"The file was classified."

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> said nothing for a long moment. The bus swung north onto Clark and the ride changed — smoother here, the street a different quality of money. <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> was six minutes out.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had been installed at sixteen. He hadn't been asked. The three surgeons and their backup protocols were already case history by the time he learned to spell NeoCortex. What the hardware could actually do under sustained low-temperature arrest, nobody knew — a useful thing to learn about yourself before you needed it to be true.

"You know what I do to people who run games on me?" <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> asked.

"I do." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> kept his voice even. The blanket was getting there; he could feel the cold edge moving into his chest, the temperature dropping in slow steps the monitor was recording for both of them. "That's not what this is."

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> looked at the readout.

"No," he said finally, in the voice of a man out of arguments. "I suppose it isn't."

The bus took the ramp to the service road. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> closed his eyes. In the hardware above his brain stem, the NeoCortex marked the thermal data, tagged the trend, and waited.

title: The Gate
text:
The <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> loading bay was lit in the flat white of a place that didn't care how it looked. <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> pulled up to the scanner gate at 0318 and idled while the death cert transmitted. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> lay under the blanket, eyes closed, hands loose at his sides.

"Core reads forty-six point two," <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> said quietly. He wasn't talking to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. He was reading a gauge on a piece of equipment he wasn't sure he trusted. "Close enough."

The monitor showed flatline — pulse off, the cardiac suppressor doing its one job. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could feel his own heartbeat the way you feel a sound through a wall: there, far off, not his problem for the next few minutes.

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> came around to the gurney. He had the paddles out. He hadn't spoken in three minutes.

"You understand," <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> said, "that the scanner confirms absence of cardiac activity. Not low. Absence." He set one paddle. Set the other. He placed them precisely — a man who was certified and competent and extremely unhappy. "This isn't a slow heartbeat I'm telling the scanner to ignore. This is a stopped heart."

"I know."

"If your hardware doesn't do whatever it does—"

"I know."

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity>'s jaw worked. He looked at the paddles, at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s chest, at the monitor. He had the face of a man who'd spent years learning not to ask certain questions and had just been handed one.

"I should throw you in the trash," he said, "you son of a bitch."

"You will," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Aim for the heart."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hand drifted toward the chest lead, checking placement. <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity>'s palm came down flat on his forearm. "Keep your hands down," <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> said. "I've run this a thousand times." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> kept his hands down.

The cold took the color first.

Then it went specific: the taste of metal on the back of his tongue, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s two fingers on his wrist in 2E at 0247 — the way her hand had felt over his pulse that time, still and professional, counting. Then the clamp came down.

Cold folded him.

He was labeled. Tagged with the case number <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> had built three days ago — male, sixty-one kilos, cause of death coronary, pending harvest review. Put in a drawer. Bay four, third tier. The drawer was exactly as narrow as promised and smelled of refrigerant and antiseptic and something deeper under that.

The last thing in the drawer with him was the count.

Eight seconds, maybe ten, where the NeoCortex was the only system still running and everything else had simply stopped, and he was, without complication, a man somebody had stopped.

Then the hardware did whatever it did.

It wasn't dramatic. No moment of waking that snapped back, no sudden breath, no resurrection. There was only the thermal log starting to record again, the cortical mesh running a location check, and his hands, in the dark, finding the bag seam without asking anything above them. His hands worked before his eyes did. His eyes caught up a little after.

The drawer was cold. He was in it.

Four hours.

He began to move.

title: Bay Fourteen
text:
<entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity>'s cooler ran in numbered bays on a grid — left to right, low to high, intake order. The lighting was maintenance-level: enough to read labels, not enough to see faces. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had memorized the floor plan from <entity repo="character" guid="019dd276-fb32-7130-bba7-08604333865f">Hua</entity>'s file, but the file was three months old and someone had shifted the grid numbering at bay six. He found the gap with his hands before he found it with his eyes.

Bay seven was where it said it was.

The tag on the bag read SCHEDULED HARVEST — <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity>'s term for a living person they had custody of and had decided not to waste. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> cut the seal at the top and worked the reversal agent through the carotid with two fingers and a syringe he'd kept sealed against his left palm for the last four hours. He'd loaded it before <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> put him under. He hadn't been sure of the loading until his hands confirmed it.

Nadia Park woke the way scientists wake from sedation — in layers, each one claiming itself back in order of priority. Orientation first. Then assessment. Her hand went to her throat before her eyes had finished finding the room — the pale of real arrest still in her face, not the theater of it. Then she looked at the thermal display on <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s chest port.

He hadn't thought about the port. The display was still running — the NeoCortex's thermal log, live, which meant she was looking at the last four hours of his arrest laid out as data: core temp floor, oxygenation curve, suspension depth, the exact signature of hardware doing something it was only supposed to be able to do in theory.

She read it for eleven seconds. He watched her read it. Not the way an intake tech reads an intake — clean, in and out, scan the slate, initial the thermal summary and move to the next drawer. She read it the way you read a curve that has stopped doing what curves do. The decline was too precise, a controlled descent, not the ragged cooling of a corpse, and then at the floor it hadn't warmed and hadn't kept falling. It had held. Something in the body had decided to stop losing heat.

"They actually built one," she said.

Flat. Not wonder — the thing a researcher says when a result she'd suspected for years and never expected to hold just arrives and has to be admitted out loud. The room smelled of refrigerant. Somewhere in the grid, a compressor cycled.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pulled the port cover closed. "Built what?"

She looked at him. Not at the port — at him. The difference was clear.

"The Atlas program had a specification ceiling." Her voice was still finding its way back to language. "A theoretical maximum. Autonomous function under zero perfusion. Not low perfusion. <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1f20-7486-94ba-e174f3f002c7">Zero</entity>." She stopped. Took a breath. "It was a number on a slide in a presentation. Nobody in the program believed you could reach it in a living system. The hardware that could hit that number was a boundary condition. Something the math allowed for and no one expected to see."

She stopped.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waited.

She didn't finish. She had answered the question under the question — the one about what she'd built — by stopping, and the stopping was its own answer. He set it aside with everything else he hadn't decided what to do with yet.

"Can you walk?" he asked.

She sat up. She tested her legs. "Yes."

"Two minutes," he said. "Then we move."

title: The Floor
text:
The supply corridor was sixty feet ahead. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had counted the bays coming in - eight on their left, thermal logs cycling green in their recessed panels. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6fa-74d9-84ad-0db8a45c43a1">Nadia</entity> was three steps behind him, close enough that he could hear her breathing through the cold. Good breath. Slow. She'd been in bad rooms before.

The patrol came around the corner at bay four.

Two men. Corpo uniforms — <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> Security, the patch with the blue caduceus. Close-quarters load: short-barreled carbines riding high on their chests. The aisle was four feet wide. He knew because he'd stepped into it with his arms at his sides and touched both bays with his elbows without trying.

The first man's hand was already moving.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the choice before the hand finished it — not the geometry, the commitment. The shoulder taking the weight, the back foot pivoting to absorb the shift of intent. The decision was already made. The man had chosen to shoot, and the choosing was done, and it hadn't cost him anything yet. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved into that half-second.

He went left, against the bay wall, and drew <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> on the short angle — no full swing, no room for one. Half-draw, <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> clearing the scabbard at twenty-two degrees and turning in the tight space between two refrigerator bays. The first man's forearm came apart at the wrist. The hand dropped with the grip still in it.

The sound <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> made in the cold wasn't what <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> expected. At minus thirty-six the air was dense and dry and the compressors were running, eating the mid frequencies, and <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>'s ring came out thin - more felt than heard. The man's scream was shorter than it should have been. The cold took it before it could form.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stepped through him, using the body as the wall it had become. The second man was backpedaling into the bay behind him — six inches more distance, opportunity not threat. The carbine was still on its sling, his hands not yet on the grip, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> closed the two steps while the man was still working out whether to draw or run.

He used the flat of <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> against the temple.

It wasn't elegant. It was the only surface that got him what he needed - down, fast, quiet - without making a second noise problem. The man hit the bay door and then the floor, and the door swung shut on its magnetic catch with a sound like a cabinet closing.

Forty seconds. Maybe thirty-eight.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in the aisle between them and took stock. The window had been tighter than it should have been. Normally the half-second was wide and clean and his — he arrived inside it with the move already chosen. The cardiac arrest had narrowed it. Tonight he'd been arriving at the edge of it instead of the center, catching the near end instead of standing in the middle. He'd had one read on the first man and started moving before he was fully set. That wasn't standard. He'd gotten lucky that the man's choice had been slow enough that arriving late still put <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> ahead of the shot.

He felt nothing about it. It was still true.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6fa-74d9-84ad-0db8a45c43a1">Nadia</entity> was against the left-hand bay, her back flat to it, both hands visible. She hadn't run. She'd stepped back into a dead corner, out of his swing, and she was looking at the two men on the floor with a face that wasn't panic and wasn't calm - the face of someone confirming a thing they hadn't wanted to be right about.

"You're degraded," she said.

"Ten percent."

"The cardiac arrest."

"Yes."

She looked at the first man - the hand, the floor around it. "He's not dead?"

"No."

"The second?"

"Concussion. He'll have a headache."

She pushed off the bay wall and fell in behind him without being asked, and they moved toward the supply corridor at a pace that wasn't a run and wasn't a walk. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> kept <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> in hand — <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> was clean, cold air and fast work - but he didn't sheathe it. Three minutes to the corridor. Two to the loading dock, where <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> was waiting with the van idling and his hands at ten and two because he'd been told to keep them there.

The compressors cycled. Behind them the bay doors stood in their numbered grid, thermal logs still tracking.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s right hand was steady. His hands were always steady - that was the hardware, keeping the tremor down below where anyone could see it while the body underneath did what it did. He wasn't sure which of them had run the fight. Maybe both. Something older than the composite had recognized the narrow aisle and chosen the short draw before he'd had any say in it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6fa-74d9-84ad-0db8a45c43a1">Nadia</entity> kept pace three steps back and didn't say another word until they reached the corridor, and by then there was nothing to say.

title: The Corridor
text:
The corridor bent left, and the four of them were already in it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stopped hard, one boot skidding on the ice-slick floor, and put his arm out to catch Nadia across the chest before she could round the corner blind. She stopped against it. Didn't ask why.

Four. Spread across the aisle in a loose staggered box — two forward, two set back, the geometry of people who'd trained past the point of bunching up in a kill zone. <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> patches. Longer barrels than the first pair. One of them had a shock-baton clipped low on the thigh, meant for a body they wanted alive.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it in under a second, the way he read everything — and the read didn't clear. It stayed open, a problem without a bottom.

Four men. Four decisions, each one running on its own clock, each one about to start whether he moved or didn't. Against one man the half-second was wide enough to live in. Against two he'd learned to split it, take the cheap one, spend the expensive one. Against four, the half-seconds didn't stack. They interfered. He could feel the arithmetic fail in real time — four barrels, four fingers, four separate moments of commitment, and no version of the aisle that let him be in front of all of them before at least one pulled a trigger.

The corridor behind him dead-ended at the bay he'd just cleared. No lateral cover. The refrigeration units were louder here, the compressors stacked and grinding, throwing frost off the door seals in a fine mist that hung and didn't fall.

He didn't have four counters. He had maybe two, clean, and after that he was standing in an open lane taking rounds and hoping the coat held.

His right hand, still around <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>'s grip, wasn't steady this time. Not visibly — nothing anyone could read off him — but he felt it himself, a half-degree of tremor under the hardware's suppression, the first crack in ten years of a thing that didn't crack.

Behind him, Nadia's breath caught and held.

The nearest man's shoulder started its turn.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> went for the wall.

He put himself against the bay door on the left, angled so only the front two had a clean line, and that bought him a fraction — not safety, just a fraction, the two rear men now shooting through their own crew's silhouette if they wanted the shot bad enough to risk it. The magnetic catch held at his spine, cold enough to feel through the coat, the compressor behind the panel grinding a slow shudder into the metal. The lead man fired. The round took the bay door six inches from <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s shoulder, and the panel spat frozen shrapnel that opened a line across his jaw before he'd finished moving.

He didn't feel the cut yet. He heard it — a small wet click, cold flesh parting cold — and filed it.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> came up in a short guard, not an attack, because there was nothing to attack yet that didn't cost more than it bought. He was out of position and knew it. Four men, one blade, one working hand, and a woman behind him with nowhere to go but back into a room with a dead patrol on the floor.

The second man was moving to flank the bay door's blind side.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had no answer ready. For the first time since the aisle at bay four, he didn't have the move already chosen. He stayed against the door and watched the four of them arrange themselves in the corridor like the answer to a question he couldn't solve.

title: The Gantry
text:
He never let himself write down, even to himself, exactly how he'd broken that fight — only that he'd reached <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity>'s rig three minutes past when the plan called for it, with no breath left to explain the difference. The supply dock at the north end took disposals around the clock. At 0740, bus 31 backed up the ramp with its running lights on and its manifest loaded. <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> came out in coveralls and moved two sealed medical-waste bags on a flatbed dolly with the ease of a man who'd done this exact job ten thousand times.

The gate clerk was a heavyset woman in a booth who'd worked overnights long enough to treat it as its own time zone. She ran the manifest, got to the bag count, and stopped.

"Says three bags," she said. "I'm looking at two."

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> didn't look at the bags. He looked at the slate and turned it toward her.

"Number transposed at dispatch," he said. "It's two. The three's a typo on the routing carbon — see the correction here, the initial." He produced a second manifest from inside his coveralls and held it out. "Had dispatch resend it at 0330. This is the clean copy."

The clerk looked at the first manifest. Then the second. Then at <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity>.

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> waited. He had the face of a man with nowhere else to be and nothing better to do, a man who'd been making night-window manifest corrections since before she was licensed. The kind of deception that worked because it was boring enough to believe.

She logged the second manifest and waved him through.

Bus 31 cleared the outer fence at 0751.

Three klicks south, <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> pulled into the shadow of a dead gantry, came back, and opened both bags. He stood over the two of them — the lunatic, and the second passenger on the manifest, tagged female, forty kilos, biohazard-flagged — and after a long moment set the empty bags back on the dolly with the care of a man putting something down he didn't mean to pick up again.

"Told you," he said, "I'd throw you in the trash."

"You did," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Best ride I've had all year."

Nadia was already on her feet, brushing residue from her sleeve with the brisk efficiency of a woman who'd woken up in a body bag before and had opinions about it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> gave her the burner. The sector address on the West Side was the safehouse where they were both headed next, not a goodbye.

She stood at the edge of the gantry's shadow a moment. Turned her head, not her body.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-ad71-7f25-a057-8e947a52b9eb">Marrow</entity>," she said.

Not a sentence. Not an instruction. The way a researcher leaves a receipt on a workbench — one artifact to say the work happened, for whoever finds it next. She didn't say anything else.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched her. In the overlay, the NeoCortex flagged the name and held it.

He climbed into the cab. <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> drove. The thermal log was still running in the overlay — he hadn't closed it, and it came to him now that he wasn't going to. The arrest interval read fifty-three seconds. Full neuretic function. No heartbeat. Fifty-three seconds of the hardware running on capacitor banks and desperation while the Governor cycled through its reset — no dropout, no cascade, no secondary arrest waiting in the queue. The curve was clean and impossible and clearly his, running from the moment <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> set the paddles to the moment his hands found the bag seam in the cold.

He watched it the rest of the way to the depot.

He thought of a counter on the North Side once, a chip pressed flat until a woman's hand covered it — the only price he'd ever insisted on paying in full, because a man who doesn't pay doesn't eat, and a man who won't pay where he's fed doesn't eat anywhere. The Qs had changed hands, half and half, exactly as agreed. That wasn't what <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> had been paid in. <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-729d-7630-8f47-5247ff773db9">Moss</entity> had been paid in a photograph he'd never get back. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had never once, in eleven years, taken a job that way. He set it next to the thermal log, in the part of him that didn't close, and didn't look at it again before the depot. Nadia was alive. The crew would have what she knew. That was all he let himself keep.

The city came up through the floor.

title: The Safe House
text:
The radiator knocked twice and went quiet.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had checked the room on the way in — habit, not nerves. Four walls, one window on the alley, a dead bolt that held, a latch that didn't. He'd fixed the latch with friction tape from his kit while Nadia was in the bathroom running water over her hands. The water ran a long time.

She came out in the clean shirt he'd left on the counter. Her own clothes were in a bag he'd burn. She sat in the chair facing the door — not the couch, not the corner — and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> noticed the choice and said nothing. Something in her wanted a sightline.

He'd made tea, because there was a hot plate and a box of something generic, and because forty minutes after a reversal agent the body sometimes needs a warm thing in its hands to believe it's safe. He set a mug on the floor beside her chair and took the couch.

She didn't touch it.

"The program ran for five years," she said. Not a beginning — a continuation, something she'd been saying in her head for a long time. "Deep-black. Spread across three CorpoNation research divisions at once. Crucible on the genomics side. A <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> subsidiary on the structural side. A third I only know by an audit code." She paused. "The split wasn't an accident. No single compliance review would ever see the whole thing. It was built so it couldn't be audited whole."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said nothing. Outside, a vehicle moved down the alley and kept going.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-ad71-7f25-a057-8e947a52b9eb">Marrow</entity> was the internal codename." Her voice was even — the scientist's cadence, careful and careful and then quickening. "I worked the architecture. Not the application. What the program was actually for, I wasn't read into. I thought it was organ-mapping. The structural work looked like organ-mapping. Detailed models of internal systems, frameworks for layered parts that talk to each other in real time." She looked at her hands. "It looked like organ-mapping."

She'd said it twice.

"Fourteen months after I left, I found a file," she said. "I wasn't supposed to be in that directory. I wasn't looking for anything. I was cleaning up an old data partition — routine — and the file was there, stored behind three deprecated directory paths. I don't think anyone meant to leave it where a person could follow the chain." She looked at the window, then back at him. "It was a recipient specification. Detailed. Behavioral modeling, identity parameters, memory architecture. The kind of document you write when you're building something that will believe things."

The radiator knocked once.

"Believe things?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"Yes." She picked up the mug and held it in both hands without drinking. "Not process data. Believe. The distinction was spelled out. They weren't building a system that handled information. They were building one that had information installed as memory — as things that had happened to it — so it would carry certain behaviors forward without ever being told to. Instructed behavior can be found and pulled. Memory looks like personality."

"The recipient specification included a trainer," she said. "A made-up figure. All of it — the sessions, the corrections, the failure points, the named techniques. Very detailed. Specific to a physical practice." She stopped. "Specific to sword work."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hands were still in his lap. The memory was there when he reached for it, exact as a photograph — the gate rig, the cold radiators, the sound of his own blade meeting the wooden post, and the correction coming in that specific tone, neither harsh nor kind. The way the man never told him why the cut was wrong until he'd already made it three times.

"There were aphorisms. Teaching phrases — the kind a student carries for years, in <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">the teacher</entity>'s voice, long after the lessons stop." She set the mug down on the floor. "I used one in the posting. After the choice, before the cost. It's in the file. Word for word." A pause. "I put it there because I needed to know if the recipient was real. It was the only way I had to find out whether the program had actually been deployed."

The room went quiet. Outside, nothing. The alley had gone still. The radiator made no more sound.

"I need to ask you something," Nadia said. "Before I tell you the rest. And I need an honest answer."

She looked at him — really looked, the way people look when they've run out of guessing and reached the place where only what's in front of them will do.

"Do you remember him? The trainer?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat with it. The grief was old and specific. He knew the third correction. He knew the sound of the phrase in a voice he had never recorded, only remembered. He knew the loss the way you only know a loss that has lived in you long enough to become part of the frame. Somewhere under it the overlay held both things at once and flagged neither — the perfect clarity of the memory, and no man attached to it.

"Yes," he said.

Nadia let out one breath — controlled, holding everything it released — and closed her eyes.

"That's the wrong answer," she said quietly. "I hoped you'd say no. If you'd said no, it meant the specification was just a draft. A design that never shipped." She opened her eyes and made herself hold his. "The trainer never existed, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. There's no man to remember. The document I found wasn't a record of a person. It was a build sheet. And every corrected failure, every phrase in that voice — you're not recalling them. You're running them. They were written to be indistinguishable from grief so that no one could ever tell them apart from the inside. Including you."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't move. The mug of tea he'd made her sat cooling on the floor between them, and the thing that had lived in him long enough to become the frame did not feel like a fabrication. That was the point. That was the horror of it — it would never feel like one.

He looked at the window, at the dead alley, at the latch he'd fixed with tape because it was the kind of thing a person did when he had somewhere real to protect. He thought about how much of what he trusted about himself he had just watched become a question he could not answer from inside his own skull.

Something in him wanted to stand up and walk out the door. Something else — quieter, and he no longer knew whose voice it was — wanted to hear the rest.

He kept his hands in his lap so she wouldn't see them.

"Then tell me," he said. "All of it. And I'll decide afterward whether I believe you — or whether that choice was written for me too."

Nadia nodded, once, and said, "Then I need to tell you what <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-ad71-7f25-a057-8e947a52b9eb">Marrow</entity> actually built."

title: What Marrow Built
text:
The radiator hummed. Somewhere above them, something cycled — a pump, an old system that had kept this room warm for years without caring what was in it.

Nadia sat with her back against the wall, the emergency blanket doing part of the work. Her hands were still. She watched him the way you watch something you designed and never expected to see standing in front of you.

"The architecture needed stability that earlier programs didn't have," she said. "The problem with composite-identity systems — systems built from many source profiles — is dissociation. You don't get a person. You get a committee. Every input hits the profiles one at a time before it reaches the integration layer, and if it doesn't clear the threshold, the response comes apart."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't move. He sat with his back to the nearest wall, <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> across his knees.

"The threshold was sixty-four," she said. "Source profiles. Below that, the integration layer couldn't hold one coherent self under high-stress input. We ran it at thirty-two. At forty-eight. The failure rate was—" She stopped and made a small motion with one hand. "Unworkable. At sixty-four it held. One functional identity, under conditions that would have shattered the earlier versions. What made it work was redundancy. Sixty-four takes on every input, agreeing, and the agreement was stronger than any single profile."

"I understand redundancy," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"I know you do." She said it quietly. "The redundancy is you."

The compressor cycled. In bay fourteen, something dripped.

"The system also needed a way to feel continuous," she said. "To make sixty-four separate parts feel like one life. Memory does that. Not synthetic memory in general — specific memory. A relationship with a history. The feeling of having been taught. Of having failed and been corrected. Of knowing someone over years."

It needed teaching phrases, too — the kind that go in deep the first time you hear them and stay, not as facts but as reflex, the hand reaching for them under stress the way it reaches for a familiar grip. It needed the profiles to agree not just on who had taught them, but on what.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was quiet a moment.

"Did the architecture include a training story?"

Not a question. Flat, the way he'd say the door opens inward.

"Yes."

"Was the trainer a real person?"

Nadia's hands shifted in her lap. She looked at them.

"The training profile was drawn from documented teaching." She chose her words the way you choose footing on ice. "Historical sources. Practitioners whose method was on record — writing, interviews, footage where it existed. The teaching voice was synthesized from that to pull the martial parts of the pool into one recognizable teacher. The profiles had to agree on how they'd been taught. They had to hear the corrections as coming from one man."

"So the method was real?"

"The method came from real practitioners, yes."

"The form. The corrections. Third correction — right wrist, last three inches of the extension."

"Drawn from documented sources, yes."

"After the choice. Before the cost. That's where you move."

Nadia went still. Then: "Yes. That one was in the file."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the sword across his knees. The blade was clean. He'd cleaned it after the corridor and hadn't once thought about whose hands had taught him to clean it, because that wasn't a thought he'd ever needed to have.

The wrist correction was right. He knew it was right because every time he ran the form his body knew it as right — not as instruction but as memory, the specific shame of a twelve-year-old who'd rolled his wrist and heard the flat disappointment of a man who'd expected better. The shame was as real as anything he'd ever felt.

"Do you know what happened to <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity>?"

He asked it in the past tense. Not: do you know <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity>. Not: is there a <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity>. What happened to him. The phrasing of a man who'd been grieving in the wrong direction for a long time and had just realized it — and realized, in the same moment, that he wasn't going to stop.

Nadia looked up. She opened her mouth. She closed it.

Something moved in her face. Not pity — pity needed a distance she didn't have, sitting on the floor of a <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> bay in a mylar blanket across from a man she'd spent three years trying to find. Not horror, either. She'd designed this. She'd run the simulations. She'd signed off on using grief as mortar.

What moved in her face was recognition.

She'd modeled the cost as a number. She had understood, in the abstract, that a made identity with an installed history would feel loss in a way you couldn't tell apart from real loss. She'd understood it as a variable.

She understood it now as a fact. The man in front of her was mourning a teacher who had never lived, and the mourning was as real as the scar the wrist correction had left in him.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waited. He was good at waiting. He was waiting now, sword across his knees, face still, for the answer to a question he already knew the shape of.

Nadia looked at him.

She didn't speak yet.

The cooler hummed.

And <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> understood, in the space where her answer should have been, that no one was going to hand him the truth of himself. He would have to go get it. Whatever <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> had been — file, footage, a dead man's method scraped into a profile — the record existed somewhere, and he was going to find where they'd built him and read every line of it, because a grief this real had earned at least the right to know its own source.

"You're holding back," he said. His voice was flat. "The file exists. You read it. You know what's in it, and you're deciding what I get to know in what order, like I'm still something that needs protecting." He stood, sword coming up with him, and crossed to the window and looked down at the alley — the same dead street, the same nothing. "You're not going to tell me. That's fine. You don't have to."

He turned back to face her.

"You're going to take me to wherever the file lives, and I'm going to read it myself. All of it. Tonight. Every line. And I'm going to know what was written into me before you get to decide which parts matter."

Nadia didn't move. Her hands stayed folded in her lap.

"If you access that partition, there will be a record," she said.

"Then there will be a record." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't blink. The decision settled into his hands the way the form did — as reflex, as certainty, as something already done. "At least this time I'll know what I'm looking at."

title: What She Knows About Seito
text:
She didn't look away from him when she started.

"The training profile was built from three sources," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6fa-74d9-84ad-0db8a45c43a1">Nadia</entity> said. Her voice was that of someone who had rehearsed this for a different audience and was finding it no easier for the rehearsal. "A pre-2200 swordsmanship lineage — instructional records, digitized, two full generations of teaching method from a Kenjutsu school outside Osaka. That was the main body of technique. Then a second-tier fighter out of the splice pool — nobody kept his name, but his teaching structure was exceptional. The way he corrected errors. The specific corrections." She paused. "And a bridge layer. Synthesized, to join the two into one arc. Nine years of it. The research showed that a sixty-four-profile system without a single anchor — one fixed point — would drift. The profiles would pull toward different norms. So the bridge had to be a person."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hands were on his knees. He didn't move them.

"The composite was given a name. A face. A voice. The death came later in the installation — grief is load-bearing, the research said. Unresolved grief around one specific person makes a stronger anchor than a living attachment. A death holds." She said it without cruelty, the way a doctor names a mechanism inside a body. "The name was a designation in the project files first. Someone made it personal during the installation."

The radiator ran on. Somewhere in the building a pipe ticked. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could hear the refrigerant moving in the walls.

"The aphorisms came from documented practitioners," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6fa-74d9-84ad-0db8a45c43a1">Nadia</entity> said. "The phrases themselves were real — pulled from verified instructors, Kenjutsu lineages, records of teaching." She let a breath out through her nose. "There's one you'll know. 'After the choice. Before the cost. That's where you move.' That was Yun-Gi <entity repo="character" guid="019ec6ef-ce8f-7013-8276-5064c33630be">Han</entity>, 2178, from a practicum in Busan. Documented. A real man. A real moment."

She stopped. She was watching him the way she'd watched him since he sat down, and she didn't look away from what came next.

"But I wrote the context. The room in Old <entity repo="place" guid="01a018a4-086e-73c5-b9ca-65a52a73f25c">Pilsen</entity>. The afternoon. The exact way he stopped the drill and said it — the pause, the turn, the light coming through the window at that angle. I put that in. The phrase was real. The afternoon I built."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't move. He stayed still a long time.

"So I'm grieving a design choice," he said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6fa-74d9-84ad-0db8a45c43a1">Nadia</entity> held his eyes and said nothing. It was the only honest answer she had.

"We should move."

title: The Claim
text:
The radiator kept time the way old buildings always did — steady, indifferent. The compressor ran a three-count.

He was standing. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6fa-74d9-84ad-0db8a45c43a1">Nadia</entity> had finished. The sources, the build, all of it — everything she had to say, she'd said. He let it settle.

Then he said it.

"I'm not even a person. I'm a meatbag haunted by dozens of ghosts." He needed her to walk it back — to draw one clean line between him and the borrowed dead, to tell him the man standing here was the original, the root, the one voice that owned the body. "So tell me which of them is me. Give me the one that's mine."

She didn't hurry to answer. She let it stand.

"Yes," she said.

That was all, for a moment.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> turned it over. Yes. Not the answer to his question — the answer to the thing underneath it. She wasn't going to draw the line, because there was no line to draw. No original. No root. Just the ghosts, all the way down, and him asking the ghosts to point at the man.

"I'll think about the distinction," he said. "When there's time for it?"

"I know," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6fa-74d9-84ad-0db8a45c43a1">Nadia</entity> said.

title: The Arithmetic
text:
The city was still doing what cities do. Three floors down, through the window, a cargo mech was backing a pallet into a loading bay. The driver stood off to the side with her arms crossed, watching the machine work — human or augmented, he couldn't tell at this distance. She'd been standing like that since <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took up the window.

He'd been at the window eleven minutes.

Nadia had stopped talking. He'd heard her stop — a sentence trailing off, then a careful quiet, the kind people make when they know the other person needs time. She was behind him, near the cot. He wasn't tracking her. He knew she was there the way you know a wall is there.

He went through it one memory at a time.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity>'s third correction: drop the elbow, find the centerline again, the stillness before the strike. Eleven days of it. He couldn't have invented eleven days — the reps were too many, too correctly spaced, exactly the kind of practice that put the result in his body. So the days had happened. The correction was real. A man had stood behind him for eleven days and watched his elbow and said the same four words in the same flat voice until <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stopped making the mistake.

The man's face, he now knew, had been assembled from a database.

He checked the elbow. The correction was still in the elbow. His body had the memory before his brain caught up, and his body didn't lie about things it had touched.

There was a girl once, on a motorcycle, in a bad neighborhood. Maybe eleven years old. She was riding it because the man who was supposed to protect her couldn't, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had been standing in the street, and she'd nearly run him down. He'd stepped aside. She hadn't said sorry. She'd looked at him from the corner of her eye the way kids look at adults they've decided are furniture, and he'd thought: she's going to be fine. Something in the way she'd handled the bike. The line she'd found through the gap.

He never learned her name. He'd been hired to keep her alive through a bad week, and he had. Φ400, paid, done. The job was real. The girl was real. Nobody had installed her. He'd been there.

He thought about a hand on his wrist. Not the whole memory. Not even a name. Just two fingers at the pulse point, someone counting. Whatever they'd counted was real — it was still there, still giving a reading. Someone had bothered to count it. That care had been real too.

So: the face was invented. The eleven days were not. The girl on the motorcycle was not. The fingers at his wrist were not.

That was not nothing. That was, in fact, most of a life.

He could keep going — the cooler floor with the thermal log still printing, the guard whose blade angle had been wrong by eleven degrees, the smell of a <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> bay at night — but the answer came back the same no matter which memory he picked up. Enough of it was real.

Down in the bay, the cargo mech finished with the pallet. The driver uncrossed her arms, checked something on a handpad, crossed them again. Waiting on a sign-off from inside the building. She was good at waiting. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched her a moment longer, then turned from the window and picked up his coat.

"You posted the job," he said. "That means they know you posted the job. We need to move."

"I know," Nadia said. "I was waiting for you to come back."

He pulled the coat on. Checked <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> out of habit — four rounds, right. "I didn't go anywhere."

"No," she said. "I know that too."

He held the door for her.

title: Why She Posted It
text:
The radiator had settled into a sound <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had stopped hearing three minutes ago — the pipes ticking, a faint drip somewhere down the hall, Nadia's breathing still working to find its own bottom. He was crouched against the shelving, his back to the cold steel, watching the door they'd come through. She sat with her spine against the next unit, close enough that he could feel her body heat as a plain fact.

He asked because he had the time and because it mattered.

"Why the open board?"

She didn't answer right away. She was the kind of person who treated a silence as a draft she could still revise.

"I couldn't use a secure channel," she said.

"You have contacts."

"I had contacts. Past tense. Anyone I could have reached inside a closed network was either already compromised or watched closely enough that reaching them would've been the same as a signed confession." She turned her head toward him, not quite meeting his eyes, looking at the middle distance the way people do when they're reciting something they worked out alone at three in the morning. "I needed someone outside every network. Someone who wouldn't need it explained. Someone who'd read the phrase and already know what it meant."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said nothing. The compressor cycled.

"There was no one else who would recognize it," she said. "It's not a real phrase. It was never published. It was never in any training record a person could reach. <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> — the construct — was private architecture. Closed source. The only place that phrase exists is in you. I put it there. I was the one who sourced the teaching aphorisms. I wanted something that would read as real to anyone who hadn't lived it, so I pulled from actual instructors. The phrase itself was real — Yun-Gi Han, a practicum in Busan, you've heard where from. But the context was mine. I wrote the room. I wrote the afternoon. I wrote <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> stopping the drill and saying it to you — the specific you, the student who needed to hear it that way."

The centerline. The correction landing. Eleven days that had never happened, in a room that had never been built, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had walked out of them knowing he'd found something. He kept his eyes on the door.

"The phrase was the only key there was," she said. "I put it in the posting — the scope line, one phrase in the requirements, nothing anyone else would read as more than flavor text. And I waited to see if anyone would recognize it. Whether the program had deployed. Whether the recipient was real. Whether he was still himself enough to read it."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched the door.

"So the job was posted to me."

"Yes."

"You just had to trust I was still working boards. Still reading."

"Still yourself enough to recognize it," she said. "Yes."

The compressor finished its cycle. In the quiet after, the cooler felt smaller.

"You could have just called," he said.

She looked at him. "I didn't have your number."

"Nobody does."

The pressure changed. Not a sound yet — a condition, the shift of a fire door opening three floors down, the building's sealed cold-chain corridors registering it as a ghost of moving air. He caught it before his ears did and had it placed between one heartbeat and the next: two bodies, moving with the gait of people who'd cleared a stairwell before.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was already rising.

"They're here," he said.

title: The Team
text:
<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> heard them at the base of the stairs.

Not footsteps. The building didn't give him footsteps. It gave him weight. The <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aae6-7e15-8bca-3992413770a8">safe house</entity> sat on a slab of reinforced concrete, and concrete carries load the way bad news travels — unevenly, but it travels. Six people. Two on the outside landing. Four climbing the stairwell in a stack. He was already moving <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6fa-74d9-84ad-0db8a45c43a1">Nadia</entity> before he said a word.

"Desk. Left side."

She moved. No question, no hesitation. He'd seen that in the cooler and again on the bus — she listened with her body first and let her mind catch up. He put her between the desk and the eastern wall. Brick. Load-bearing. Three feet clear of the window's line. Then he crouched beside her and kept his voice low enough to die in the drywall.

"Two on the fire escape. They'll hold the east window until they hear the front door go. Don't move until I tell you. If I say run, you go through the bathroom, out the window, into the courtyard. You don't look back to see what's behind you."

She nodded once. Her eyes tracked the room — not panic, the calm of someone who had already pictured exactly this ending for weeks. He noted it and set it aside. There'd be time to be surprised by her later, or there wouldn't.

He went to his coat on the hook by the door.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> came free of the holster with a sound he knew the way he knew gravity. He checked <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">the cylinder</entity> by feel. Four rounds. He'd spent two inside <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> and reloaded one in the corridor. Four was what he had, and four was a number, and a number he could work with.

The stairwell went quiet.

That was the signal. Professionals stop moving right before they move — the last weight on a step, then nothing, then the door.

The door came in on a ram, low and fast.

He didn't wait for it to stop.

The first two rounds went through the upper panel at angles he'd already worked — the door frame, the spacing of a breach team, where the point man's chest had to be at full stride. The shotgun's spread did the rest. The point man dropped into the doorway. The second man caught the edge of the pattern and spun sideways into the frame, still up, still moving, one hand on his weapon.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was already sliding left.

The fire-escape crew took the east window on the sound of the shots. He'd figured six seconds. They came in four, which told him they were better than the pair at the door, and that fact landed somewhere under his ribs before he'd finished the thought. <entity repo="material" guid="ef551a9f-9fe5-f0ce-0769-797d4c4f0822">Glass</entity> blew inward. Two shapes, low and fast, spaced like men who had done this together.

Two rounds left.

He put one into the near shooter at seven feet. Center of the chest, nothing fancy. The second was already through the frame with an angle on <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6fa-74d9-84ad-0db8a45c43a1">Nadia</entity>, which meant the desk wasn't cover anymore. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> fired his last round as he closed — not to hit, just to push the man's aim wide — then got inside the reach of the gun, where a gun is a liability. The scabbard came up before the sword cleared it.

It wasn't clean. He drove the pommel end into the man's throat, blade still sheathed, the angle bad because the man was already lifting an elbow to block. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the block land — actually felt it, a jolt he hadn't priced for — and had half a second where the whole shape of the exchange came apart in his hands. He turned the strike down instead of through, ramming the low end of the scabbard up under the ribs. The man folded. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took him by the collar and put him into the wall, and the man stopped being a problem.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> came free.

The second man at the door had his weapon up and a ruined shoulder — the shotgun had done enough. Twelve feet, a narrow room, furniture between them. A pistol is slower than a man who already knows where you'll be. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved before the trigger finger finished deciding, past the furniture line, the overhead cut already committed when the arm came up. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> answered the arm and then answered him.

The room went quiet except for the building settling.

He stood still for three seconds and counted.

Four in the stack. Two down inside, one on the threshold, one he couldn't place. He went low to the doorframe and checked the stairwell. Nothing. Either the fourth had held outside and was already gone, or he was somewhere in the building <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> couldn't reach from here. He held for two more seconds.

Nothing moved.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6fa-74d9-84ad-0db8a45c43a1">Nadia</entity>'s voice came from behind the desk, steady. "There's a coat."

He turned. She had his coat over one arm, held out to him — his left arm, the one that needed to be free. She'd taken it off the hook during the fight. He didn't know when. She'd been reading the room the whole time, on her own map, and she'd done the right thing at the right second without being told, and that landed somewhere he didn't have a place for yet.

He took the coat.

"Can you walk?"

"Yes."

"Then we're leaving."

He scanned the room one more time. Not for comfort. For inventory. All four rounds gone. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> clean. The fourth man still a question. His left shoulder had a new catch in it, the arm that had driven the scabbard paying for the angle. The hit he'd taken in the <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> corridor had been grinding on his lower ribs through every exchange and was doing something worse now — two cracked, maybe one broken. It would matter tomorrow. It didn't stop him tonight.

He said nothing about any of it.

The coat went on over all of it.

"The stairs," he said, and she was already moving.

title: After
text:
The contractors were in the stairwell, the hallway, and the chair where he'd left one of them. He counted them before he counted himself.

Six. All there.

Then he checked his own body, the way a mechanic walks a chassis after a hard run — not hunting for one thing, just finding what had changed. Left side: two ribs cracked, maybe one broken. The shoulder he'd driven the scabbard with had locked up tight, worse now than it had been ten minutes ago, a wrench deep in the joint that biotape wouldn't touch but that he'd pressed on anyway in the dark, in the forty seconds he'd had. His hands were steady. His neuretics ran hot — he could feel the heat at the base of his skull, the small stubborn headache that meant he'd burned past what the read cost him — but the overlay was still up and still readable. He was working.

Nadia stood against the far wall, arms folded, watching him.

"Count's done," he said. "You're not hurt."

"No."

"<entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> will know the team went dark. They'll wait maybe ten minutes for a check-in, then send a runner to confirm. After that someone senior decides what this becomes." He picked the slate up off the table where she'd set it. "You've got about forty minutes before that call gets made. Be somewhere I don't know about before it does."

She watched him. "You planned this before they came."

He handed her the slate. A sector address in Z4. A transit code that would clear two checkpoints without a flag. A name. "The contact holds for seventy-two hours. Don't go back to wherever you slept last night."

She looked at the slate. Then at him — the same look she'd had in the cooler reading the thermal log, finding something still running that she hadn't expected to.

"You need a doctor," she said.

"I know one."

She didn't push. She wasn't a person who pushed at things already decided.

A silence. Not an uncomfortable one — just the room being what it was now. Someone else's <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aae6-7e15-8bca-3992413770a8">safe house</entity>, safe for thirty-nine more minutes.

"The phrase in the posting," she said. "<entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity>'s phrase. I used it because you were the only one who'd know it." She paused. "I didn't know if you'd still be —" She stopped. Started again. "I didn't know if you'd still be yourself?"

"I'm not sure that's the right word."

"I know," she said. "I used it anyway."

She tucked the slate inside her jacket, precise about it, the way she'd been precise about everything he'd watched her do tonight — the bay numbers in the cooler, the way she moved when he told her to move. She had been waiting a long time, he thought, to be moving again.

She went to the door and stopped with her hand on the frame. Without turning she said, "The man they built is the one who came. I don't think they knew that's what they were building."

Then she was gone.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in the room.

He didn't go to the window. She'd earned an exit no one watched.

He went to work. He moved the contractor nearest the door out to the stairwell — not because it would matter in forty minutes, but because tidiness was a habit, and habits don't take the night off. He picked up the casings by count, his neuretics tagging each one as it went in his pocket. He wiped the surfaces he'd touched. He checked the way he'd come in and made sure it still looked like a door no one had used.

The shoulder was bleeding again, slow, through the biotape — a slow leak, nothing urgent. Something to manage on a clock. His left arm he kept loose at his side, where it wouldn't catch on the coat; looking at the leak made it real in a way that changed how his body moved, and he needed his body to move clean for the next part.

He had the doctor's code ready in the overlay. He'd send it two blocks out and moving.

The phrase. It was <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity>'s, and <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> was a design document, and the phrase had been written into him by people who needed the pieces to fit. He'd known that for four hours now. He turned it over — not for new information, just to set the weight of it down in the right place.

The man they built is the one who came.

He didn't know if she was right. He wasn't sure the question had a right answer. The sword still knew what his hand knew. Whatever the sixty-four had been built to make, it had held. Whatever word she'd reached for and set aside — yourself — it pointed at something still in the room. Still working. Still willing to hold a count.

He thought that was enough.

He picked his jacket up off the floor, thumbed two fresh rounds into <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> from the pocket, and left.

title: The Form
text:
The stairwell smelled like mildew and mineral water, from a pipe that had been weeping through the wall since before the ferrocement wave. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stopped on the third-floor landing. Not because anything needed it — nothing was coming, he'd checked twice — but because his hands were doing something without him.

The right hand. His sword hand.

It had moved into the first position of the third correction, the grip adjustment <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> had drilled into him across three hundred repetitions on a specific Tuesday he couldn't find now. He had a sense of wooden floors. Slant light. A clear memory of being told his elbow was too high. A less clear memory of the face that told him. And no memory at all of the afternoon it got fixed — because that afternoon never happened. The correction that mattered, he'd worked out himself, two years later, when he noticed the form dragged the cut slightly sideways.

He'd fixed it alone. On a job. After the job. Standing in an alley on the north side with a body cooling behind him and nothing but time.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> never saw the change.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> ran the form once on the landing, slow, no urgency. Weight shift, turn at the hip, the drive through the shoulder, elbow where he'd decided it belonged instead of where he'd been told. The form was better now. Cleanly, plainly better.
