Whoever built the <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> construct had done it from archives — recordings of a thousand real fighters folded into one teacher, the way you'd render a face from ten thousand faces and get something no mother would recognize. Good work. Real work. The skill had arrived in him whole and true. But the archive didn't hold the alley on the north side, or the job before it, or the four hundred times he'd done the grip wrong in the two years after <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> before he caught it himself.

None of that was installed.

He ran the form to the end. His hands came back to rest.

He had a grief with no object. He'd known <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> nine years — which wasn't true in any sense a court would take, and the grief was real anyway, which was maybe the point. The afternoons were invented. The form was his.

There was a second grief under the first. A master, even a made-up one, is someone else's certainty to lean on. Masterless meant no certainty but his own. On the page that sounds like freedom. On a cold landing at four in the morning it felt like a house with the load-bearing walls pulled out. He'd need his own answer soon, about <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> — whether to send her back from a door he hadn't cleared, the thing <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> would have demanded and the thing that would get her killed. He'd choose for himself instead. That was the whole of what masterless left him to give her: not a master's certainty, just a man deciding, alone, and carrying what the deciding cost.

He decided on the landing, then, before the next flight took the choice out of his hands. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> stayed. He'd bring her through the uncleared door at his shoulder and eat the risk himself, because the man <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> never finished building was the one who had to answer for her now, and that man had just run a form nobody taught him and found it good. He'd tell her when he reached the street. No more deferring it to a floor he hadn't walked yet.

He sheathed <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>.

Two more flights, a fire door, and then <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the gray zone</entity>, and <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the gray zone</entity> gave him north-side asphalt at four in the morning. The texture of it was older than anything in his design files. Cracked expansion joints spaced wrong. A repair crew's aggregate that didn't match three blocks in either direction — the split feed showing in the pavement itself, one substation's contractor laying one grade and the next block's laying another, nobody owning it cleanly, which was why it stayed neutral. He'd learned this ground by walking it, not by being built with it. The city kept collecting in him whether he asked it to or not.

The next job was already waiting. He knew the address. He knew roughly what it would cost — not the money, the money was simple, but the read-budget, the sword-hours, the shoulder that would need two days before he could drive it hard again. He knew the ground going in. He knew there were things he didn't know. There was always a variable.

He'd run the form. The form was better than what he'd been taught. That felt like an answer, though not the kind that closes anything.

It was better because he'd fixed it in the gap. <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> — whoever built him — made the decision, laid the foundation, drilled three hundred Tuesdays into a hand that would never stop moving. <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-185c-7752-b83e-baa921571078">Seito</entity> had known the Way. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had learned that the Way had a thousand small deviations, and that the deviations were where you actually lived. Then the cost of that building came due slowly, over years, in alleys and jobs and a drag on the cut no archive had predicted. Between the choice and the cost, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had lived. That gap was where the adjustment happened. That gap was where he'd been living his whole life without knowing it had a name.

He kept walking.

The city made its north-side sounds — a freight slug pulling under the street, the low hum of a cooling tower three blocks east, something with wings and no sense stuck in the gap between two buildings. None of it needed anything from him. The first gray light was starting to turn the ferrocement the color of old water.

He was on his way to the next job. It would have its own costs, its own variable. This was what happened after. This was the whole of it.

He already knew how to move in it.

Somebody stole <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s motorcycle.

He stood in the alley behind <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity> at 06:40 with a cup of tea going cold in his hand and laid the facts out where he could see them, because they refused to add up. Fact: the alley had one entrance, and the entrance had a camera, and the camera worked, because <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> kept it running in exchange for the landlord ignoring what her power meter did. Fact: the wheel hub had been locked. Fact: the plate cover — his plate cover, the one he folded a particular way — sat on the concrete where the bike used to be, folded the particular way.

Folded. Not dropped. Whoever took the bike had pulled the cover off first, folded it like laundry, and left it as a receipt.

He stood in the mouth of the alley for a count of four. Not looking for movement — looking for the shape of what had happened. No drag marks on the asphalt. No cut chain, no stress marks, no tool scatter, no cigarette ends. The hub lock lay open where he'd left it locked, cycled clean, the mechanism sealed again like it had never opened at all. Professional work. The kind that doesn't leave bread crumbs.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> drank some of the cold tea and let himself feel the thing he was feeling, which was not, strictly, professional. He'd owned the bike nine years. He'd bought it with his second fee ever — the first had gone to a flat with a door that locked — and it was the only thing he'd ever bought that wasn't a tool. The bike was not a tool. The bike was the long way home. It ran on H-cell power and mechanical linkages, no telemetry, no smart systems, nothing to trace, and that was why it mattered — eleven years in this city and his whole inner life had a displacement of 1200cc, and some polite person had walked it out of a locked alley under a working camera between 03:00 and dawn.

He went back upstairs and knocked on 2E.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> opened the door with a soldering iron in one hand and yesterday's hair. She read his face the way she read his walk.

"Who died?"

"The bike's gone."

She went very still. Then she set the soldering iron down on the little shelf inside the door, the one she kept for the moments when something needed both her hands, and said, in the voice she used for load-bearing bolts:

"Somebody boosted my work?"

"Your work?"

"Who do you think built the anti-theft — the manufacturer? The manufacturer's anti-theft was a sticker." She was already pulling her boots on. "The hub lock is mine. The ignition handshake is mine. Three years, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>, nobody's gotten past the handshake — I'd have heard, I read the forums, people complain about me by name."

"Lock's still there," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Cycled open. Not forced. Opened."

That stopped her, one boot half-laced. "No ping?"

"No ping."

"There's supposed to be a ping." She said it slowly, the way you say a thing to hear whether it's still true out loud. "You crack the handshake, the hardware locks down and burns the mechanism and screams at me from across the city. That's the whole design. You don't get through quiet." She finished the lace by feel, eyes somewhere past the doorframe, running the numbers he could see her running. "Whoever did this didn't break it. They talked to it. They asked it what it wanted to hear and it believed them, and then it closed the door behind them like a gentleman."

She grabbed her field coat.

"This isn't theft. This is peer review."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was already moving toward the stairs when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> caught her arm.

"The camera footage."

She stopped. The hand he had on her sleeve was steady, but his shoulder wasn't—he'd favored it since the stairwell, and now the weight of the decision he'd just made was settling into the muscle. He let go.

"Thirty-one minutes of nothing," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. Not a question. She was already running the math. "03:12 to 03:43. Clean gap. Somebody upstream with the right permissions held the feed."
